title: ICE removes Venezuelan colonel and human rights violator
description:
“ICE officers continue to remove human rights violators to their home countries,” said ERO Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston.
“This removal reflects the outstanding work of ICE Miami, HSI Miami, FBI Miami and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center.
The case was supported by ICE Miami, HSI Miami, and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center.
During the same period, ICE has obtained deportation orders against, and physically removed from the United States, 1,178 known or suspected human rights violators and facilitated the departures of an additional 208.
The Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center has issued more than 80,000 lookouts for potential perpetrators of human rights abuses and has stopped more than 415 human rights violators and war crimes suspects from entering the United States.
text:
MIAMI — On Aug. 18, ICE removed Rafael José Quero Silva, a known human rights violator who participated in the detention and torture of political dissidents during the Maduro regime, to Venezuela following a Department of Justice immigration judge’s order of removal.

ICE arrested Quero Silva, an illegal alien from Venezuela, Feb. 27, 2025, in Miramar. He entered the United States June 20, 2016, at Miami International Airport but failed to depart in accordance with the terms of his admission.

“ICE officers continue to remove human rights violators to their home countries,” said ERO Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston. “This removal reflects the outstanding work of ICE Miami, HSI Miami, FBI Miami and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. We are committed to public safety and national security, and to ensuring the United States does not become a safe haven for individuals who participated in persecution, torture or other serious human rights abuses.”

“HSI remains committed to working with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and hold accountable human rights violators who seek refuge in the United States,” said HSI Miami Special Agent in Charge Jose R. Figueroa. “This case reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting the integrity of our immigration system and ensuring that individuals who participated in persecution or torture cannot evade justice.”

Prior to entering the United States, Quero Silva served as a colonel in the Bolivarian National Guard of Venezuela, known as the GNB, commanding the 47th Detachment in the city of Barquisimeto. He was involved in, and had knowledge of, the excessive use of force, detention and torture of anti-Maduro protesters by GNB members under his command. Reports indicate that in 2013, Quero Silva directly oversaw the torture of at least 74 peaceful demonstrators. While in the custody of Quero Silva’s 47th Detachment, these political protesters were subjected to electric shocks, severe beatings with nightsticks and frozen water bottles, threats of rape, and other physical, psychological and sexual abuse.

The case was supported by ICE Miami, HSI Miami, and the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center. The HSI-led Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center furthers the government’s efforts to identify, locate and prosecute human rights abusers in the United States, including those who are known or suspected to have participated in persecution, war crimes, genocide, torture, extrajudicial killings, female genital mutilation, or the use or recruitment of child soldiers.

Since 2003, ICE has arrested more than 520 people for human rights-related violations of law under various criminal and immigration statutes. During the same period, ICE has obtained deportation orders against, and physically removed from the United States, 1,178 known or suspected human rights violators and facilitated the departures of an additional 208. The Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center has issued more than 80,000 lookouts for potential perpetrators of human rights abuses and has stopped more than 415 human rights violators and war crimes suspects from entering the United States.

text:
Christian Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week, asking a federal judge to prevent the sheriff in Cameron County, Texas, from releasing Castro, and to order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.

WATCH: ICE agent kills Mexican immigrant in Houston in latest deadly enforcement encounter

Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

At a federal hearing in Brownsville on Tuesday, attorneys with the Minnesota Attorney General's Office argued it would be hard to compel Castro to face charges in their state if he is released, and they fear Castro may flee the country, citing his phone conversations with a woman who lives in Mexico.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

title: Data shows sharp increase in ICE arrests across Maine - WGME
description:
ICE has arrested more people in Maine so far this year than in the previous two years combined, according to new data released by a national nonprofit.
The Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition published the Maine data in its own report.
Also read: Report: Most people arrested by ICE in Maine operation had not been convicted of crimes The data shows a sharp increase in detentions this year, with roughly 482 arrests in Maine so far in 2026.
Earlier this year, CBS13 reported that just half of the arrests made by ICE in Maine were targeted.
In the newly released data, DHS removed that distinction.
text:
ICE has arrested more people in Maine so far this year than in the previous two years combined, according to new data released by a national nonprofit.

The data also shows the vast majority of people detained did not have a criminal record.

According to the Deportation Data Project, roughly 2% of individuals detained in Maine between January and July of this year had a criminal history. Only one person had a violent criminal conviction.

"It's one person. You probably have a better chance of finding a needle in a haystack," said Ruben Torres, director of advocacy and policy for the Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition.

The Deportation Data Project collects immigration data from the U.S. government and makes it publicly available. The Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition published the Maine data in its own report.

Also read: Report: Most people arrested by ICE in Maine operation had not been convicted of crimes

The data shows a sharp increase in detentions this year, with roughly 482 arrests in Maine so far in 2026.

Torres says there have been about two arrests every day since May, forcing families to have difficult conversations.

"How do you tell a 4-, 5-, 6-year-old you're gonna be the man of the house if dad is arrested?" Torres said.

"What has been sold to the public as a need for public safety isn't being reflected in how the actions are being undertaken," he added.

DHS previously said it was targeting people it called the "worst of the worst."

Earlier this year, CBS13 reported that just half of the arrests made by ICE in Maine were targeted. The rest involved individuals who were near an ICE agent and suspected of being in the U.S. illegally.

In the newly released data, DHS removed that distinction.

When asked why, DHS did not directly answer the question but said in part:

"Many of the individuals that are counted as 'non-criminals' are actually terrorists, human rights abusers, gangsters and more; they just don't have a rap sheet in the U.S. Further, every single one of these individuals committed a crime when they came into this country illegally."

DHS also disputed the report's accuracy and said the data in question was not reviewed before it was released.

Also read: 'Operation Catch of the Day': ICE launches major enforcement effort in Maine

The data was obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests.

Torres hopes state and federal leaders use the information to push for significant immigration reform.

"Find ways to fund a functional immigration system. That way, going through the process actually means something for families," Torres said.

Based on the volume of calls to an immigrant hotline, Torres believes arrests are on pace to continue increasing through the end of the year.

He says he hopes making the data public will empower the community and promote government transparency.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained almost 50,000 people in July, marking its highest monthly arrest total during President Trump’s second term, newly released data shows.

According to numbers published in the Deportation Data Project — a joint project conducted by the University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Los Angeles — ICE arrested 49,571 people in July 2026. A Monday Associated Press analysis noted that the figure marked a surge in detainments, jumping by 15 percent from the month prior.

For the majority of 2026, detention numbers stagnated around the lower 30,000 range. Detainments in July jumped by 70 percent from when this plateau began in February.

Since the Trump administration’s February immigration crackdown in Minnesota, called Operation Metro Surge, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have expanded their enforcement across the country. The agencies have also invested heavily in their officers as President Trump rolls back deportation protections for several migrant groups.

Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, was deported Monday — marking the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty military member who was removed from the country.

“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez told the AP. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities — but also take care of my family.”

Navy sailor Joshua Aviles — currently serving aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which earlier this month faced scrutiny for declining living conditions — similarly reported that his father had been detained by ICE. After Aviles’s social media pleas, his father was released from custody Wednesday.

“I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” the sailor wrote in his initial post.

ICE also deported more than 160 immigrants to Haiti last week, acting on a June Supreme Court ruling that allowed the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for around 330,000 Haitians and more than 6,000 Syrians.

But polls suggest public approval of ICE’s expanded efforts is dwindling. In early August, the AP and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that Americans’ approval of Trump’s handling of immigration had dropped by 10 percentage points since the start of his second term, reaching a 58 percent disapproval rate.

text:
By Vince Gasparini

syracuse.com

SYRACUSE, N.Y. — Fifteen county sheriffs across New York state have filed a lawsuit over a state law that bans local law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement.

The suit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York on Tuesday. Among those suing the state are Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood and Oswego County Sheriff Don Hilton, according to court papers.

| SPECIAL REPORT: Find the hidden gaps in your agency’s logistics readiness

Gov. Kathy Hochul is named as a defendant in the lawsuit, alongside Attorney General Letitia James and the state of New York.

The law, dubbed the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act,” was signed by Hochul in May. The suit was filed Tuesday, the same day the law took effect.

The law prohibits local authorities from entering into formal or informal cooperation agreements with ICE. It also bans local jails, juvenile detention centers and youth detention facilities from holding people on civil immigration charges.

When the bill was signed, Hochul argued that it was necessary due to what she says is the out-of-control nature of the operations being carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The lawsuit argues that the agreements between ICE and the sheriffs are sanctioned by the U.S. Congress and that no state executive has the authority to tell sheriffs — as elected officials — that they cannot participate in the agreements.

Onondaga County Sheriff Toby Shelley was not among the sheriffs named in the lawsuit. Not long after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Shelley told syracuse.com | The Post-Standard that he would not comply with the president’s requests to have his deputies work with ICE in their immigration enforcement.

“I took an oath to protect people’s constitutional rights,” Shelley said. “Everything this sheriff’s office does is going to be legal. We’re not going to hold anyone illegally.”

The department also has a policy that goes back at least a decade that bars deputies from questioning people about their immigration or citizenship status.

Hood, however, has not been shy in his support of Trump’s immigration crackdown and mass deportation agenda.

In July 2025, he entered the Madison County Sheriff’s Office into a 287(g) agreement, which allows the Madison County jail to detain people otherwise due for release and hand them over to federal agents for civil immigration violations.

His activism on immigration enforcement, along with opposition to bail reform and other criminal justice reform, landed him a spot as the running mate of Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive and Republican nominee for governor.

In July, the Attorney General’s office warned Hood to end his agreement with the federal government. While he agreed to end the 287(g) as required by the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act,” he said he still intends to work with ICE and honor its requests to detain and hand over any undocumented immigrants that come into custody at the county jail.

After the Tuesday lawsuit was filed, Hochul and James released a statement saying that the suit is “nothing but a frivolous waste of taxpayer dollars.”

“The courts have already declined to block this law once, and we are confident they will do so again,” the statement reads. “In the meantime, we expect all law enforcement agencies in New York to uphold state law.”

Here are the sheriffs suing the state:

Broome County: Sheriff Frederick Akshar

Cattaraugus County: Sheriff Eric Butler

Cayuga County: Sheriff Brian Schenck

Delaware County: Sheriff Craig DuMond

text:
Activity from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has spiked in the last two days, particularly in Danbury and Stamford, according to public officials and activists. Monday morning, agents were seen at Kennedy Park in Danbury arresting men who were day laborers, according to activists, and they returned Tuesday to make more arrests.

The agency has released no public information tied to the apparent arrests, although videos have been popping up on social media that include people being handcuffed in the street, on sidewalks and in parking lots before being taken away in vehicles. It is unclear where they were taken or what followed.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations,” an ICE spokesperson said by email in response to a request for comment from CT Insider.

“Under President (Donald) Trump and Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.,” said the email sent from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The circumstances have put the community on edge, officials say. Officials in Danbury have not had contact with ICE and could not confirm any arrests, Taylor O’Brien, chief of staff for Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, said. Officials in Stamford did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Tuesday. Alves, in a video posted on Facebook, encouraged immigrants to know their rights in these situations.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"First day of school and a lot going on and a community that is scared. A community that is scared to go to work, a community that's scared to send their kids to school, a community whose kids are scared to go home and have a parent missing because of the ICE operations yesterday and today throughout our state, but more heavily here in Danbury," said Alves, who is also the Democratic Party state chairman.

The lack of public information has led to community activists trying to collect any information they can in an effort to quantify the arrests and lend support to those arrested and their families. There have been over 20 arrests in Danbury in the past two days, according to Carolina Bortolleto, who is with the advocacy groups Greater Danbury Area Unites for Immigrants and CT Students for a Dream. In Stamford, organizer Marcella Branca with Stamford Norwalk United with Immigrants said there have been at least six arrests, although ICE has not confirmed any of them.

There is little publicly available information on ICE arrests, which have spiked this summer, according to the Associated Press The Trump administration has reportedly sought to reach a total of at least 2,000 arrests a day nationally, the New York Times reported. Both outlets said the arrests are an indication of the administration's mass-deportation agenda being followed through on.

The agency will sometimes release details of individual arrests, but it only does so voluntarily. ICE doesn’t generally release arrest reports or other similar records. And the people it arrests generally have their cases heard in immigration court, where case files are not open to the public.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Olga Guerra hadn't spoken to her husband, Fidel Romero, since she says federal immigration agents arrested him and a coworker on their way to work in Stamford early Monday morning, leaving his empty truck sitting outside a convenience store.

Romero was among the two dozen, or so, people believed to be arrested by ICE in the roundups the past two days. He has three children with Guerra.

“I tried my best right now to tell my kids to be strong as well, and dad is going to be fine,” Guerra told CT Insider on Tuesday afternoon during a phone interview, her voice cracking with emotion. “I don’t know. I feel like there’s no right words right now.”

The operation continued Tuesday, which was the first day of classes for public schools in Stamford and Danbury. Branca said she saw men wearing ICE vests in two vehicles facing a school bus stop Tuesday morning in Stamford while children waited to be picked up.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It was honestly very unsettling, to see the two cars facing the kids going to their first day of school,” Branca said. “It’s not a nice thing to see.”

The Stamford Public School District is aware ICE has had an increased presence in the city, spokesperson Kathleen Steinberg said.

“We want to reiterate that Stamford Public Schools welcomes all children, regardless of race, religion, gender, disability, socioeconomic background or immigration status,” Steinberg said in a statement. “We are grateful to our community partners and the SPS Welcome Center staff who are working hard to provide support to students and their families who have been impacted by the recent ICE activity.”

The Danbury Public Schools did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Immigrant rights groups and local residents have posted several videos online that show ICE agents taking people into custody Monday and Tuesday, often in the middle of the street.

A video posted to Facebook on Tuesday showed five ICE agents attempting to wrestle a man’s arms behind his back as he was lying on the street in front of a preschool center in Danbury, his arms folded underneath him.

“You’re going to get sprayed,” a masked agent said on the video as he pointed a canister of what appeared to be pepper spray at the man’s face.

“Put your arms out,” another agent said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Two other videos sent to CT Insider showed what appeared to be at least five unmarked law enforcement vehicles parked in the street near a preschool center, with federal agents getting in and out of the vehicles.

In separate videos posted to Instagram by Greater Danbury Area Unites for Immigrants on Monday, what appeared to be a lone ICE agent wrestled with a man in the middle of the street next to an auto shop as he told the man to stop resisting. A second agent then ran over to assist.

Later in the same video, the first ICE agent can be seen holding a Taser over the man as he lies prone on the street with his arms handcuffed behind his back. It’s not clear from the video whether the officer deployed the Taser.

title: Leger Fernández Leads 18 Members Demanding Answers on Trump Administration's Rush ...
description:

7923, which established a 10-mile mineral withdrawal surrounding Chaco Canyon.
“Chaco Canyon is not just a historical site; it’s a living cultural landscape,” the lawmakers wrote.
During a June 2025 House Natural Resources Committee hearing, Burgum committed to Leger Fernández to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct individual, in-person consultations with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco Canyon.
The Department also provided only 21 days for public comment and held no public meetings before advancing its proposal.
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Ranking Member of the House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian and Insular Affairs, and Congressman Jared Huffman (CA-02), Ranking Member of the House Natural Resources Committee led 18 members of Congress in demanding answers from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum about the Trump Administration’s rushed effort to revoke protections for lands surrounding Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

The Department of the Interior is proposing to revoke Public Land Order No. 7923, which established a 10-mile mineral withdrawal surrounding Chaco Canyon. Revoking the order would reopen these culturally significant public lands to oil and gas leasing and mining activities.

“Chaco Canyon is not just a historical site; it’s a living cultural landscape,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Department’s current fast-tracked efforts to overturn the withdrawal area do not respect the historical, cultural, and spiritual value of Chaco Canyon.”

“The Department’s rushed review undermined the Department’s trust responsibility to Tribal nations and the Tribal consultation process under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act,” they continued.

The lawmakers’ letter raises serious concerns that the Department failed to fulfill its trust responsibility to Tribal nations and honor Burgum’s public commitment to meaningful consultation. During a June 2025 House Natural Resources Committee hearing, Burgum committed to Leger Fernández to send an official with decision-making authority to conduct individual, in-person consultations with every Tribe with an interest in Chaco Canyon. However, Interior’s own draft Environmental Assessment indicates that the Department moved forward before completing all requested consultations. Several Tribes received only “informational meetings,” while requests to meet with a decision-maker remained unmet.

The Department also provided only 21 days for public comment and held no public meetings before advancing its proposal. Despite that abbreviated process, the public submitted an estimated 300,000 comments.

By contrast, the existing protections were finalized in 2023 following 150 days of public comment, eight public meetings, and years of advocacy by Tribal nations. An archaeological study identified more than 4,730 cultural sites within the protected area.

The lawmakers are asking Burgum to disclose:

● How many Tribal consultations included an Interior official with decision-making authority;

● Why the Department failed to honor Tribal requests to meet with a decision-maker;

● Why Interior published its draft proposal before completing Tribal consultation;

● Whether all requested consultations will occur before the Department completes its review; and

● Why Interior conducted a limited Environmental Assessment instead of a more comprehensive Environmental Impact Statement.

The lawmakers requested answers by Friday, August 28.

The letter was signed by Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández, Jared Huffman, Melanie Stansbury, Gabe Vasquez, Sharice Davids, Betty McCollum, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Mark DeSaulnier, Val Hoyle, Donald Beyer Jr., Judy Chu, Dina Titus, Jesús “Chuy” García, Sylvia Garcia, Rashida Tlaib, Diana DeGette, Julia Brownley, and Raja Krishnamoorthi.

She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.
Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.
She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch.
text:
Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal.

Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes.

One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van.

According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle.

Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport.

Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April.

An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.”

“ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email.

The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.”

The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed.

The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data.

Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation.

“We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said.

‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’

Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.

“I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.”

Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. She and other members connected with these groups to learn about monitoring the flights.

Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.

“What’s new in the last couple of years is just the fact that … these people aren’t getting their due process,” Muth said.

Maureen Newton of the Burley/Rupert area recently went to the airport to watch a flight for the first time. She said she’d read about the flights and had concerns about it.

“This is my taxpaying dollars here I’m watching go down the garbage can,” she said, keeping her eyes on the plane as detainees with their hands bound in front of them boarded the plane one at a time.

Shelly McDaniel records a video of the boarding process for each flight and later takes a screenshot of each person who boards. She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch. The goal is to make the information available to attorneys so they can find their clients.

McDaniel and her husband told the Sun they are supportive of people with criminal convictions being deported, but their concern is that the detentions and deportations happen too quickly for the court process to finish. Shelly McDaniel said she

“I know of people that have been taken on a Sunday, and on Tuesday they’re on a plane,” Shelly McDaniel said. “… there’s just no way they’re even able to present their case in court.”

Twin Falls Republican state Rep. Clint Hostetler told the Sun in an email he’s supportive of the flights and argued that due process is being followed.

He said he supports “the rule of law, and that includes enforcing our nation’s immigration laws.”

“My understanding is these operations prioritize individuals who have already gone through the legal process and received a final order of removal, it also includes people with criminal convictions, public safety concerns, or no valid legal status to remain in the country,” Hostetler said. “This isn’t a new or extraordinary policy, it’s the law being applied.”

He said he understood that the flights could be “unsettling to some in our community, but failing to enforce the law isn’t fair to the people who came here the right way, or to Idaho taxpayers.”

“My focus as a representative is on what’s best for Idaho families and communities,” he said, “and that includes a secure, lawfully enforced immigration system.”

Attorneys must file a Habeas petition in court with jurisdiction before detainee is moved

If an attorney is going to be able to stop a detention before someone is deported and get a chance to argue their client’s case in court, they often must obtain what is called a habeas corpus petition.

Habeas petitions allow people to challenge their detention in court.

Twin Falls attorney Brian Tanner said attorneys for detainees must file for a habeas in a court with jurisdiction over where the detainee is located.

“You have to know immediately where they are, because you have to provide notice to the district court that you are filing habeas so that they don’t send them out, or you have to get them before they leave,” Tanner said.

If the petition is filed in time and someone is flown out anyway, that person has to be returned, Tanner said.

Shelly McDaniel said she’s seen at least one person leave on a plane and return later.

Prior to 2025, those who were apprehended by federal immigration authorities in the interior of the United States and who hadn’t committed a separate crime typically had the ability to get a bond hearing and avoid detention.

Tanner said before the flights began, a bus with the area’s detainees would leave on Wednesdays and eventually take them to an immigration court in Utah. Tanner could often secure his clients’ release before they left.

However, the U.S. Department of Justice under the Trump administration has changed its policy and began using a federal law typically only used for people who are caught while crossing the border or who just crossed the border, which allows them to be held without bond.

He said the no-bond policy reinterprets how immigration has been enforced for “decades and decades and decades.”

This new policy has been challenged and, at the end of July, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel of judges ruled that the government couldn’t withhold bail. Other circuit courts in other regions have had mixed rulings regarding this policy, with some upholding it and others blocking it, Stateline reported.

Tanner’s frustration with the recent major changes in the system have led him to limit how many immigration cases he’s taken. He’d previously practiced immigration law for nearly 20 years.

“Immigration is constantly changing in so many different ways. The president has an influence. The courts are basically interpreting laws in different ways. It’s always moving,” Tanner said. “So we get a different president, but I’ve never seen anything like this.”

ICE flight observers helped someone find detained family member, hope to help more

McDaniel said she recently saw a post on social media about someone trying to find their family member after he was detained in Idaho Falls. McDaniel reached out to ask her what he was wearing when he was detained and shared some photos with the person that matched the description.

McDaniel used the screenshots of detainees boarding flights and was able to help to find the family member near Tacoma. The person who posted was then able to try and find a lawyer in the area.

“It was very nice to know we were able to help them,” McDaniel said.

Muth, the Indivisible leader, said the plan is to try and keep monitoring and let people know what’s happening at their local airport.

“I think it’s always good to hear what everyone thinks about them, and to be able to have civil discourse, to talk about it,” Muth said. “… we do notice people are either one way or another. So they’re either for the flights and they’re happy that it’s happening, or they’re just extremely upset. And there can be a lot of emotion on both sides.”

text:
Denver— Colorado U.S. Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper joined U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen and six of their Senate colleagues to demand answers from the Trump administration about recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) actions in airports. This inquiry comes after a string of incidents nationwide, in which ICE agents – with apparent cooperation from TSA – have targeted people at airports, including at Denver International Airport.

“We write to express our serious concerns regarding recent immigration enforcement actions at airports across the nation conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), with the apparent assistance and support of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA). Such actions create fear in our communities and cause disruption and distress to the traveling public,” wrote the senators.

“Unfortunately, recent reporting by the New York Times indicates that troubling events like these are occurring frequently across the nation at America’s airports. Such actions have only served to disrupt local communities, create fear among immigrant families, and undermine the travel and tourism sector by actively discouraging travelers from visiting the United States. They hurt our nation’s travel and tourism industry at a time when it is trying to rebound from a 5.5% decline in international tourism in 2025 that occurred due to President Trump’s misguided tariff, immigration, and foreign policies,” continued the senators.

Bennet has consistently fought against the Trump administration’s inhumane immigration policies. This month, Bennet and Congressman Jason Crow (D-Colo.) led all Democrats in the Colorado Congressional delegation to call on the GEO Group to comply with public health orders issued by the Adams County Health Department and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment related to an active tuberculosis case at the ICE detention facility in Aurora. Bennet and his staff have joined Crow and his congressional office in conducting consistent oversight visits to the Aurora detention facility throughout the current administration. In their most recent visit on August 14th, staff at the facility said there were no active cases of tuberculosis. This month, Bennet also joined U.S. Senator Mazie K. Hirono (D-Hawaii) and U.S. Representative Judy Chu (D-Calif.) to introduce the Protect American Values Act, legislation that would prevent federal funds from being used to implement, administer, enforce, or otherwise carry out the Trump administration’s finalized “public charge” rule.

In July 2026, Bennet joined U.S. Senator Angus King (I-Maine) and 37 of their Senate colleagues in calling for stronger accountability measures for ICE officers. In May 2026, Bennet introduced three bills aimed at reforming the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including ICE and Customs and Border Protection: the Keeping Immigrants and Destinations Safe (KIDS) Act; the Training, Responsibility, Uniforms, and Standards for Transparency (TRUST) Act; and the Oversight, Protection, and Enforcement Notification (OPEN) Act. In March 2026, Bennet issued a statement when Trump fired former Secretary Noem, and emphasized that DHS must undergo a complete overhaul. In January 2026, Bennet joined his colleagues in introducing the Providing Useful Budgets for Localities to Invest in Cops by Substituting Appropriations from Federal Enforcement To Yield Results Act, legislation to redirect nearly $75 billion in funding passed in the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act from ICE and send it instead to local law enforcement programs to help hire and train 200,000 local police officers in communities across the country.

In November 2025, Bennet joined his colleagues in introducing the bicameral Restoring Access to Detainees Act, legislation to ensure DHS allows noncitizens who have been detained to contact their legal counsel and families. In August 2025, he joined the Immigration Enforcement Identification Safety Act to prohibit immigration enforcement officials from wearing masks and to require them to wear visible identification. In February 2025, Bennet joined his Senate colleagues to introduce the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, which would reinstate DHS’ long-standing policies to prevent ICE from making arrests at sensitive locations like schools, hospitals, and places of worship.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Mullin, Administrator Cummins, and Acting Director Venturella:

We write to express our serious concerns regarding recent immigration enforcement actions at airports across the nation conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), with the apparent assistance and support of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA). Such actions create fear in our communities and cause disruption and distress to the traveling public. It is further alarming to read recent reports that ICE and TSA have a formal agreement to share passenger information with each other, which could be used in immigration enforcement at airports. We therefore request that you provide Congress and the American people details about any information sharing agreements that are in place between ICE and TSA and ask the Department of Homeland Security and its component agencies, ICE and TSA, to let us know what concrete steps you are taking to ensure all immigration enforcement agents conducting operations at airports operate solely based on active judicial warrants, wear and utilize body cameras, wear and display clear identifying information, and refrain from wearing masks, which shield ICE from accountability for abuses and instill fear in travelers.

Just a few weeks ago, masked and plain-clothed ICE officers attempted to violently arrest an elderly man at the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas (LAS), without any identification, before running off following public intervention. Even more recently, ICE arrested a pregnant woman at the same airport, separating her from her fiancé. News reports indicate similar enforcement operations are taking place at Reno-Tahoe International Airport (RNO), Denver International Airport (DEN), and San Francisco International Airport (SFO) as well. Additionally, the recent detention of several Marylanders, including a medical researcher and former Fulbright scholar and a pharmacy professor, both asylum-seekers traveling domestically with lawful documentation, raises serious concerns that ICE’s expanded presence at airports is subjecting law-abiding individuals to detention.

Unfortunately, recent reporting by the New York Times indicates that troubling events like these are occurring frequently across the nation at America’s airports. Such actions have only served to disrupt local communities, create fear among immigrant families, and undermine the travel and tourism sector by actively discouraging travelers from visiting the United States. They hurt our nation’s travel and tourism industry at a time when it is trying to rebound from a 5.5% decline in international tourism in 2025 that occurred due to President Trump’s misguided tariff, immigration, and foreign policies. Additionally, these actions are increasingly targeting individuals who have expired visas, even though many such individuals often have a legitimate pending application for a visa extension or renewal with USCIS. With a backlog of nearly 12 million visa applications at USCIS, visa processing delays are impacting the ability for USCIS to process a variety of visas, employment authorization documents (EAD) applications, and renewals in a timely manner, meaning that a person can have an expired visa with a legitimate pending application yet still be detained by ICE at an airport due to visa processing delays that are out of their control.

News reports also indicate that according to a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) recently obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request, ICE and TSA have a formal framework to coordinate the sharing, storage, and management of passengers’ sensitive information. This is particularly concerning because Acting TSA Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill claimed during congressional testimony she gave in January 2026 that TSA does not send information to ICE; however, the MOA appears to directly contradict that statement. Of similar concern, when just last month then TSA Administrator nominee David Cummins was asked about the conduct of ICE agents at America’s airports in questions for his nomination hearing, he did not even attempt to answer how he would or would not work with ICE if confirmed to the role.

With all this in mind, we request your response to several questions regarding the operating relationship between ICE and TSA and the type of information that is being shared between the agencies. We look forward to a prompt response to this inquiry.

Is there an official process in place to ensure that local airports are aware of an impending immigration enforcement operation?

Does the information-sharing agreement between ICE and TSA require ICE to provide proof that the individuals they are requesting information about have active warrants for their arrest? Does this information-sharing agreement distinguish between judicial and administrative warrants, and is such a warrant a requirement for TSA to cooperate with ICE in enforcement actions at airports? If this information is sensitive, then we ask for a member or staff level briefing to receive this information in a classified or secure setting.

According to the MOA, TSA shares data with ICE that ICE then stores in its own repository. What specific data is shared between the two agencies? What criteria is being used, either with or without this data, to determine when to conduct an immigration enforcement operation at an airport?

Reporting indicates TSA shared information on more than 31,000 travelers, leading to more than 800 immigration-related arrests. Please provide a breakdown of what information caused the 800 individuals to be arrested, and how many people were detained for an expired visa that had an application pending with USCIS, including information on how many of these arrests led to a deportation? Additionally, if a warrant was issued for those arrested, please also provide a breakdown of how many arrests were based on ICE having a judicial versus administrative warrant.

What safeguards are in place to protect passenger privacy and ensure that the individuals being targeted in enforcement operations at airports are dangerous or violent criminals and not merely immigrants who have followed the law and have had a temporary lapse in status solely due to USCIS processing delays?

Does TSA have any policy regarding how law enforcement agencies such as ICE are to identify themselves when they are in an airport or when they are attempting to take an enforcement action in an airport?

Do DHS, ICE, or TSA factor in the impact on domestic and international travel that enforcement operations could have when planning their execution? Have DHS, ICE, TSA, or any other agency or official in this administration been in contact with travel and tourism industry leaders and experts to ensure that such actions do not negatively harm our travel and tourism industry?

We look forward to your prompt response to these questions. Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

More than half of the nearly 50,000 arrests came from four states: Texas, Florida, California and Georgia.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded 49,571 arrests in July, setting the highest monthly arrest total in President Trump's second term, according to recently released government data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

The total surge averages out to 1,599 apprehensions a day, and tops June's record-breaking number of 43,021 arrests by 15%.

Since taking over in March, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pivoted from the confrontational style of immigration enforcement of his predecessor, Kristi Noem. The former head of DHS often accompanied ICE officers on high profile raids, including Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, which left two American citizens dead at the hands of federal agents. Instead Mullin pledged to fulfill the Trump administration's deportation goals while keeping the department out of the headlines. The latest data is reflective of a strategy that is working.

Graeme Blair, co-director of the Deportation Data Project says the uptick is due to Mullin's change in tactics.

"What we're seeing is an expansion in all of the different ways that ICE is detaining people," Blair told NPR. "They're arresting people at airports, at ICE check-ins, at immigration courthouses and this is the result of that."

Blair also noted that the latest figures include the initial wave of arrests of Haitian immigrants whose Temporary Protected Status was revoked in July.

text:
Here are the morning’s top stories on Tuesday, August 25, 2026

The Trump administration’s deportation policies are separating families across the country. For some children left behind, that separation can take a serious toll on their mental health and wellbeing. Here in California, nearly 5 million people live in mixed status households where at least one family member is undocumented. Today, we’re diving deeper into how immigration arrests are affecting children and their communities in Los Angeles with Cora Cervantes, a reporter with MindSite News.

Nearly 300,000 K-12 students experienced homelessness last school year, a 10% increase since the last recorded peak in 2019.

A bill that would make it easier for people to sue federal agents for civil rights violations has advanced in the legislature.

This interview had been edited for legth and clarity.

You spoke with children directly affected by the immigration raids and arrests. What has their experience been like living through these mass deportation policies?

CERVANTES: Yes, I did, I spoke to children, from toddlers all the way to teenagers. And despite being so young, the impact that the raids have had on toddlers is very apparent. Like in the case of one little boy, he is very aware that his dad is not with him. I got to sit down with him and watch him play and the entire play time, he kept on talking about Papi the whole time. “Donde esta Papi? Where is Papi?” So you see the absence. And in teenagers, I noticed a state of what some experts called parentification. So them trying to parent their younger siblings or parent their parents, in terms of keeping them calm and reassuring them that things are going to be okay. And so I saw a mix of a lot of things, but basically a lot anxiety, signs of depression, and decreased sense of security and self.

It sounds like that’s taking a real toll on their mental health, but you also report about their physical health as well.

CERVANTES: Well, it has an impact on their physical health as well, because they’re interrelated. The stress and anxiety that we feel, it translates to the way that our body operates, from like our heart rate to the quality of our sleep. And obviously that not only impacts their physical health, but that translates to their learning outcomes, their everyday quality of life. And so you do see that in them as well.

And you’ve touched on it briefly, but when kids don’t feel safe in their communities, what are some of the consequences of that?

CERVANTES: I spoke to psychiatrists and social workers that work with these families. And so one of the things that really stayed on my mind, especially for younger children, is as they’re starting to build attachment, they don’t build secure attachment in a community that feels unsafe. And that translates to their ability to relate to others, to build relationships with others. So it really ruptures a complete sense of trust in others and themselves. And so this impacts their ability to open up to learning new things, whether it be at school or simple things like maybe a sport they might play or an art activity they could have engaged in that completely closes them off.

And you mentioned kind of some of the short term impacts, but what are longer term impacts of these immigration raids on kids and their families?

CERVANTES: These children are potentially at long-term risk of not just the toxic stress, but the physical and mental illness that emerges from it. They will face higher risks of substance abuse, depression, higher suicide rates, difficulty establishing relationships in their lives. And so, all of that’s compounded with already existing challenges that they may face in relation to poverty, or safety issues in their community. So it’s just this layer on top of layer that then yields an adult that will have a lot of challenges, both economically and emotionally, in the way they navigate the world. All of this is leaving a long-term, potentially multi-generational impact on these families. And on a very human level, that’s just enough for people to be concerned from a community standpoint. But if we think about it from a societal, from an economic standpoint, like we’re rupturing entire communities and security for everybody.

text:
On August 25, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) that would impose a new $103,265 fee on H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those filed under the advanced degree exemption. The proposal would effectively codify and make permanent the Trump administration’s earlier $100,000 H-1B fee initiative, which was imposed by presidential proclamation in 2025 but subsequently blocked by a federal district court. The proposed fee would be payable at the time of filing and would be in addition to existing H-1B filing fees and surcharges. DHS estimates the fee would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually.

Unlike prior USCIS fee increases, DHS proposes using revenue from H-1B cap filings to fund activities across multiple federal agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), the Department of State (DOS), and the Department of Labor (DOL). The proposal would allocate the projected revenue as follows: approximately $3.0 billion to USCIS, $3.0 billion to EOIR, $1.2 billion to DOL, $1.05 billion to ICE, with smaller allocations to DOS and CBP. DHS states that these funds would support activities ranging from adjudications, fraud detection, and vetting to immigration court operations, labor certification programs, and visa-processing functions.

This fee funding structure represents a departure from USCIS’s historical fee-setting approach, where USCIS fees have traditionally been tied to the costs of adjudicating immigration benefits. Here, DHS is proposing shifting broader immigration-system costs to employers filing H-1B cap petitions based on its determination that such employers are better positioned to absorb the additional expense than other immigration benefit requestors.

The NPRM provides a 30-day public comment period. The proposal arises amongst the backdrop of ongoing litigation over the administration’s previous $100,000 H-1B fee. In June 2026, a federal judge ruled that the fee was unlawful and barred the government from collecting it. The administration has appealed that decision, and further judicial review remains pending. As a result, legal challenges to DHS’s authority to impose a fee of this magnitude are widely expected if the rule is finalized.

If finalized, the proposal would represent a dramatic increase in the cost of sponsoring new H-1B workers in the annual cap (previous government costs were between $2,000-$6,000 depending on employer size and whether expedited processing was requested). As such, the additional fee could significantly affect employer demand for H-1Bs and workforce planning.

text:
A federal judge in New York has struck down the federal government’s policy that suspended immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries. The court found that the State Department exceeded its legal authority by imposing a blanket restriction based on nationality and ruled that immigrant visa applications must be reviewed on an individual basis.

What Was the Policy?

Implemented in January 2026, the policy directed U.S. consulates to stop issuing immigrant visas, including many family-based and employment-based immigrant visas, to nationals of 75 designated countries. The government stated that the policy was intended to address concerns that applicants from those countries were more likely to become dependent on public benefits.

What Did the Court Decide?

The court held that U.S. immigration law does not allow the State Department to deny immigrant visas solely on the basis of nationality. Instead, visa eligibility must be determined through an individualized review of each applicant’s circumstances. As a result, the court vacated the policy and ordered the government to stop relying on it when adjudicating immigrant visa applications.

What Does This Mean for Applicants?

For now, individuals from the affected countries should have their immigrant visa applications considered on a case-by-case basis rather than being denied under the 75-country restriction. The ruling may also allow for reconsideration of certain applications that were previously refused under the policy.

The court’s decision restores individual review of immigrant visa applications and rejects a nationwide nationality-based restriction on immigrant visa issuance. The Administration is expected to appeal the decision, meaning additional litigation is likely. However, until a higher court rules otherwise or issues a stay, the State Department’s 75-country immigrant visa suspension is no longer in effect.

title: Alex Pretti's family calls for accountability 7 months after fatal CBP shooting - NewsNation
description:
The family of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse who was fatally shot by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during a January crackdown on immigration in Minnesota, called for answers from the Trump administration on Tuesday — seven months after his death.
Steve Schleicher, an attorney for the Pretti family, told ABC News that the family deserves to know who shot their son and that that person or persons should be prosecuted.
The Department of Justice opened a civil rights investigation into the shooting shortly after Alex Pretti’s death, pledging to work in tandem with the FBI and a division of the Department of Homeland Security.
The FBI had previously said it would not share evidence related to Alex Pretti’s death with Minnesota investigators.
“My aim has always been to ensure justice is done, and this evidence-sharing is a positive development in that essential work,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said after obtaining the footage.
text:
The family of Alex Pretti, the ICU nurse who was fatally shot by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents during a January crackdown on immigration in Minnesota, called for answers from the Trump administration on Tuesday — seven months after his death.

“I was not shocked that he helped somebody. My shock is that he was murdered and no one has given us the complete truth or anyone has been held accountable,” his mother, Susan Pretti, told ABC News‘ George Stephanopoulos during a “Good Morning America” interview. “And it’s been seven months.”

Witnesses of the shooting said they saw the slain nurse recording immigration officers with his cellphone while trying to help up a woman who one agent had pushed down. Law enforcement officials then surrounded the 37-year-old, with one appearing to wrestle Pretti’s firearm — for which he had a permit — away before two agents fired several shots at him.

The Hennepin County Medical Examiner ruled his death a homicide. But, while the two officers were charged for use of force, they have not been charged for the killing.

Susan Pretti, sat alongside her husband Michael Pretti and daughter Micayla Pretti, added that there was “more effort in vilifying him than pursuing justice, investigating this.”

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem accused Alex Pretti of being involved in an “act of domestic terrorism” for endangering the agents’ lives, mimicking her description of Renee Good — a Minneapolis resident killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers earlier the same month.

Other Trump administration officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, called Alex Pretti a “domestic terrorist” and an “assassin.” President Trump himself wrote on Truth Social that ICU nurse was “perhaps” an “insurrectionist.”

“It’s so un-presidential,” Michael Pretti said. “It’s ridiculous that, you know, the leader of the free world speaks that way about an American citizen.”

His father added that their son cared about his community and was only observing immigration officials’ activity in Minneapolis, not protesting against them.

“We’ve seen what happened,” Michael Pretti noted. “The videos are pretty clear. But we want justice. We want accountability for the people that did this to Alex.”

The family learned about his death while watching news coverage of immigration enforcement in the city, seeing footage of “our son be shot 10 times on TV,” the father said.

“What did he do to deserve to be murdered?” Susan Pretti asked. “To be left cold, on the ground, dead, my child? What did he do?”

She asked why the family “should not get” an apology.

Steve Schleicher, an attorney for the Pretti family, told ABC News that the family deserves to know who shot their son and that that person or persons should be prosecuted.

The Department of Justice opened a civil rights investigation into the shooting shortly after Alex Pretti’s death, pledging to work in tandem with the FBI and a division of the Department of Homeland Security.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, then serving as deputy attorney general, said prior to announcing the probe that Alex Pretti’s actions did not match “the legal definition of domestic terrorism.” After the announcement, Blanche added that he was “not committing to anything with respect to that investigation.”

Last month, Minnesota officials obtained body camera footage and other evidence from the federal government of the shootings of both Alex Pretti and Good. The FBI had previously said it would not share evidence related to Alex Pretti’s death with Minnesota investigators.

“My aim has always been to ensure justice is done, and this evidence-sharing is a positive development in that essential work,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said after obtaining the footage.

More than a dozen New York sheriffs are suing over a state law prohibiting law enforcement from entering into or maintaining certain agreements with ICE for civil immigration enforcement, as Gov. Kathy Hochul dared the agency heads to "bring it on."

A federal lawsuit led by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault argues that the law is unconstitutional and unlawfully restricts elected sheriffs’ ability to enter into federally authorized immigration-enforcement agreements.

"Today, Kathy Hochul escalated her administration’s war on the police and she expanded polices to put criminals before the citizens of New York," Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin said on Tuesday.

The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, which Hochul signed in May, took effect on Tuesday, barring local and state law enforcement agencies from entering into partnerships with federal authorities to assist on civil immigration matters. The law also bars new agreements to house civil immigration detainees; existing detention agreements must be terminated under their applicable termination provisions within three months of the law’s effective date.

BORDER CZAR HOMAN VOWS TO 'FLOOD' NEW YORK WITH ICE AGENTS DESPITE HOCHUL'S RESISTANCE

Police may still assist ICE in cases of violent or other forms of non-immigration crime, but officers may not divert local resources to help with civil immigration enforcement as part of an effort to advance President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.

"No county executive should think that they are above the law in the state of New York," Hochul said at a press conference on Tuesday.

"And to those suing us, those trying to block the implementation of this law who’ve tried before and failed, our law has already been upheld by the courts, but if you try me again, I say, bring it on," the governor declared.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS

New York Attorney General Letitia James also issued subpoenas to law enforcement agencies that either did not confirm plans to end their agreements or failed to provide what her office viewed as a satisfactory response. "Because we need local cops hunting down criminals, not kindergartners. Breaking up drug rings, not breaking up families. Arresting gun runners, not grandmas," Hochul said.

title: 20 states sue Trump administration for threatening safety grants over immigration compliance
description:

The lawsuit also accuses the Trump administration of not considering how denying these grants would undermine public safety across the country.
“Action by this Court is urgently needed,” the lawsuit states, asserting that it is illegal for the administration to impose these conditions on the public safety grants.

text:
The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) has joined 19 other states, including the commonwealths of Massachusetts and Virginia, in a lawsuit pushing back against the Trump administration’s attempts to attach immigration enforcement requirements to federal grants supporting state and local public safety efforts.

About a year ago, 20 states filed a similar lawsuit over Trump administration FEMA funding cuts, showing a pattern of states challenging federal grant conditions.

“Threatening to cut funding that supports law enforcement if states don’t agree to unlawful conditions is an abuse of the Trump administration’s authority,” Attorney General Josh Kaul said in a statement. “This funding should be distributed to the states, not improperly used as a bargaining chip.”

The lawsuit states that the grant programs, which have been active for decades, “provide more than a billion dollars to States annually to address some of the most serious threats to the safety of their residents: from gang violence to drug trafficking to sexual assault to all kinds of violent crimes.” The funds, which are enacted by Congress, are used “to assist more than 8.5 million crime victims; pay more than 200,000 claims for losses suffered by crime victims; and fund ongoing criminal justice and public safety operations, such as drug task forces, crisis intervention programs, and youth recidivism reduction efforts, in all 50 states and over 1,000 local government units nationwide,” the lawsuit states.

Under President Donald Trump, states which depend on these funds have been advised to either cooperate with Trump’s immigration priorities or face losing access to those funds. Calling this a “brazen attempt to manipulate critical funding for law enforcement and crime victims to strong-arm States into supporting the Administration’s civil immigration policies,” the lawsuit asserts that the Trump administration is running afoul with governing principles of the United States: that a federal agency “has no power to act … unless and until Congress confers power upon it.” Since Congress has the power of the purse, it decides what criteria executive branch agencies — like the Justice Department — must use when awarding grants, the suit argues.

The lawsuit also accuses the Trump administration of not considering how denying these grants would undermine public safety across the country. “Action by this Court is urgently needed,” the lawsuit states, asserting that it is illegal for the administration to impose these conditions on the public safety grants.

In a press release, the Wisconsin DOJ said Monday that last year the Trump administration declared that states wouldn’t be able to access Victims Crime Act funds unless they cooperated with the administration’s hardline deportation agenda, affecting $1.3 billion in grants.. A coalition of states sued and the administration reversed its action and released the money.

This year, however, the immigration conditions have been applied funding for juvenile justice and law enforcement, and amount to over $6 million in Wisconsin alone — a loss of $3.2 million in grant assistance, $2.1 million for a crisis intervention program, and $800,000 for juvenile justice and delinquency prevention, according to DOJ.

Although 20 sheriff offices across Wisconsin partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through the 287(g) program, many communities have mixed relationships with the controversial federal agency. Some police departments may still cooperate with immigration enforcement even without an official 287(g) program. Others have policies prohibiting officers and jails from participating in immigration enforcement.

Despite public pushback, immigration agents have conducted surges and arrests in neighborhoods, courthouses, and elsewhere since Trump returned to office. In Milwaukee County, where some of these enforcement efforts have played out, local elected officials have enacted local ordinances and policies to curb the effect ICE operations have on public safety in the city. These, however, have invited further confrontation with the Trump administration.

description:

Agency officials claim this will ensure visa applicants will not end up relying on US public benefits.
This week the Trump administration also announced plans to revoke visas from asylum seekers who had initially entered the US for tourism or business.
“The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center, said.

text:
Good morning. All US immigrant visa applications have been paused by the Trump administration as the state department moves to tighten restrictions and limit access to applicants whom they deem could need US assistance. The agency launched the initiative at all embassies and consulates in early August.

Applicants with scheduled interviews were sent emails that their appointments had been canceled. Agency officials claim this will ensure visa applicants will not end up relying on US public benefits. This week the Trump administration also announced plans to revoke visas from asylum seekers who had initially entered the US for tourism or business. Up to 200,000 people seeking asylum could be affected.

Is the move lawful? “The court made clear that immigration laws cannot be used to justify discrimination,” Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Law Center, said. In February, a federal judge overturned the president’s attempt to suspend the US refugee system entirely.

Instagram CEO denies company hid low use of teen safety feature in Meta trial

Adam Mosseri, the first senior Meta executive to testify in a historic lawsuit brought by 29 US states, disputed allegations by US prosecutors that his company hid negative information from the public in a court in California.

Questioned over touting a feature called Take a Break, meant to encourage teens to close Instagram if they had been scrolling for a while, Mosseri was asked about not disclosing low user numbers for features geared toward teen safety. He brushed the concerns aside, saying: “We don’t publish every single stat. I’ve definitely said publicly that the opt-in rates are low. I don’t know if I’ve said numbers.” Just 1.8% of teens signed up for the feature.

Why are the states suing Meta? The lawsuit centers on the allegations that Meta deliberately designed addictive products that hooked young people, leading to mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and suicide. Meta has denied all allegations, saying the states are chasing an “outlandish payout”.

At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward

At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals. The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.

Dr Aneza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, said 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that “one baby was saved by a doctor”. Women who had just given birth were forced to run down several flights of stairs to evacuate. Investigators were still at the scene and authorities have not confirmed the cause.

How have authorities responded? The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an ​immediate investigation. “Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” said Sharif. “Those responsible should be identified and the strictest action should be taken.”

Trump threatens to demolish Kennedy Center if $250m renovation not done

The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could be demolished if repairs are not carried out, the Trump administration has warned in a court filing. Lawyers for the US president said the national arts complex in Washington DC must undergo a $250m renovation or risk facing the wrecking ball.

The threat emerged on Monday as the administration urged a federal judge to reject a fresh legal challenge to Trump’s efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center. The dispute has become part of a months-long battle over the president’s attempt to alter the memorial created by Congress in honor of John F Kennedy. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

What other changes has Trump already made in Washington DC? Trump has demolished the East Wing of the White House to make way for a $600m ballroom and ordered a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool that resulted in algae blooms and a peeling liner. The Kennedy Center board has voted to change the building’s signage to read: “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump.” It also voted to name the grounds the “President Donald J Trump Plaza”.

In other news …

South Carolina voters have chosen Darline Graham as the Republican nominee for US Senate. She overcame concern about her lack of legislative experience to beat the five-term congressman Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s Republican special primary runoff.

An Ecuadorian mother and daughter were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at a hospital after a car crash in central Florida.

A polygamous sect leader serving a 50-year federal sentence for orchestrating sex involving children was given another 24 years in prison on separate state convictions for child abuse.

The father of a US navy sailor who has been deployed on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been released from immigration detention, according to his family.

Stat of the day: At least 47 killed and dozens kidnapped in gang attack near Haiti capital

At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once peaceful community near Haiti’s capital. A gang leader has threatened to kill hostages if authorities kill any gang member, piercing the belief that security in the Caribbean country was improving.

Well Actually: 11 gym dos and don’ts from fitness experts

Hogging weights? Loud grunting? Sweaty benches? Here’s what professionals have to say about good workout etiquette, from using equipment to being on your phone.

Don’t miss this: Dolly Parton, country star, actor and philanthropist, remembered

The world feels a little dimmer today without Dolly in it after her death was announced by her nephew Bryan Seaver on Instagram. We have lots of coverage worth spending a little time with – an appreciation of her music by critic Alexis Petridis, a wonderful gallery of her life in pictures, a selection of her greatest quotes, Hannah Marriott writing on Parton’s unique fashion style, and a list of her 10 best recordings. You can share your tributes and memories of the country music icon with us too. Rest well, Dolly.

Climate check: Record-breaking heat dome expected to bring dangerous temperatures to US south-west

Surging temperatures are expected to broil more than 45 million people as a heat dome settles across the south-western US through the end of August and into early September, according to the National Weather Service.

Last Thing: Call to ban marmot hunting in France as campaigners say they are ‘killed for fun’

Animal rights campaigners are gearing up for protests and petitions aimed at persuading the French government to ban the hunting of Alpine marmots. Although the marmot is not a threatened species, its numbers are reportedly declining as a result of the climate emergency. Campaigners say they are opposed to them being hunted for fun.
