title: Twin Falls ICE flight observers record more than 500 detainees flown out of Magic Valley airport
description:
The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April.
Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’ Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said.
She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.
Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.
She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch.
text:
Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal.

Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes.

One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van.

According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle.

Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport.

Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April.

An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.”

“ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email.

The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.”

The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed.

The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data.

Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation.

“We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said.

‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’

Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.

“I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.”

Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. She and other members connected with these groups to learn about monitoring the flights.

Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.

“What’s new in the last couple of years is just the fact that … these people aren’t getting their due process,” Muth said.

Maureen Newton of the Burley/Rupert area recently went to the airport to watch a flight for the first time. She said she’d read about the flights and had concerns about it.

“This is my taxpaying dollars here I’m watching go down the garbage can,” she said, keeping her eyes on the plane as detainees with their hands bound in front of them boarded the plane one at a time.

Shelly McDaniel records a video of the boarding process for each flight and later takes a screenshot of each person who boards. She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch. The goal is to make the information available to attorneys so they can find their clients.

McDaniel and her husband told the Sun they are supportive of people with criminal convictions being deported, but their concern is that the detentions and deportations happen too quickly for the court process to finish. Shelly McDaniel said she

“I know of people that have been taken on a Sunday, and on Tuesday they’re on a plane,” Shelly McDaniel said. “… there’s just no way they’re even able to present their case in court.”

Twin Falls Republican state Rep. Clint Hostetler told the Sun in an email he’s supportive of the flights and argued that due process is being followed.

He said he supports “the rule of law, and that includes enforcing our nation’s immigration laws.”

“My understanding is these operations prioritize individuals who have already gone through the legal process and received a final order of removal, it also includes people with criminal convictions, public safety concerns, or no valid legal status to remain in the country,” Hostetler said. “This isn’t a new or extraordinary policy, it’s the law being applied.”

He said he understood that the flights could be “unsettling to some in our community, but failing to enforce the law isn’t fair to the people who came here the right way, or to Idaho taxpayers.”

“My focus as a representative is on what’s best for Idaho families and communities,” he said, “and that includes a secure, lawfully enforced immigration system.”

Attorneys must file a Habeas petition in court with jurisdiction before detainee is moved

If an attorney is going to be able to stop a detention before someone is deported and get a chance to argue their client’s case in court, they often must obtain what is called a habeas corpus petition.

Habeas petitions allow people to challenge their detention in court.

Twin Falls attorney Brian Tanner said attorneys for detainees must file for a habeas in a court with jurisdiction over where the detainee is located.

“You have to know immediately where they are, because you have to provide notice to the district court that you are filing habeas so that they don’t send them out, or you have to get them before they leave,” Tanner said.

If the petition is filed in time and someone is flown out anyway, that person has to be returned, Tanner said.

Shelly McDaniel said she’s seen at least one person leave on a plane and return later.

Prior to 2025, those who were apprehended by federal immigration authorities in the interior of the United States and who hadn’t committed a separate crime typically had the ability to get a bond hearing and avoid detention.

Tanner said before the flights began, a bus with the area’s detainees would leave on Wednesdays and eventually take them to an immigration court in Utah. Tanner could often secure his clients’ release before they left.

However, the U.S. Department of Justice under the Trump administration has changed its policy and began using a federal law typically only used for people who are caught while crossing the border or who just crossed the border, which allows them to be held without bond.

He said the no-bond policy reinterprets how immigration has been enforced for “decades and decades and decades.”

This new policy has been challenged and, at the end of July, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel of judges ruled that the government couldn’t withhold bail. Other circuit courts in other regions have had mixed rulings regarding this policy, with some upholding it and others blocking it, Stateline reported.

Tanner’s frustration with the recent major changes in the system have led him to limit how many immigration cases he’s taken. He’d previously practiced immigration law for nearly 20 years.

“Immigration is constantly changing in so many different ways. The president has an influence. The courts are basically interpreting laws in different ways. It’s always moving,” Tanner said. “So we get a different president, but I’ve never seen anything like this.”

ICE flight observers helped someone find detained family member, hope to help more

McDaniel said she recently saw a post on social media about someone trying to find their family member after he was detained in Idaho Falls. McDaniel reached out to ask her what he was wearing when he was detained and shared some photos with the person that matched the description.

McDaniel used the screenshots of detainees boarding flights and was able to help to find the family member near Tacoma. The person who posted was then able to try and find a lawyer in the area.

“It was very nice to know we were able to help them,” McDaniel said.

Muth, the Indivisible leader, said the plan is to try and keep monitoring and let people know what’s happening at their local airport.

“I think it’s always good to hear what everyone thinks about them, and to be able to have civil discourse, to talk about it,” Muth said. “… we do notice people are either one way or another. So they’re either for the flights and they’re happy that it’s happening, or they’re just extremely upset. And there can be a lot of emotion on both sides.”

text:
A federal judge in the Eastern District of Michigan on Friday dismissed a lawsuit alleging that Washtenaw County’s “sanctuary policies” were illegal.

In her opinion, Judge F. Kay Behm stated that “neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will,” adding that “the government cannot otherwise compel localities to enforce the President’s priorities in the manner it wishes.”

She wrote that the federal government cannot compel states or local governments to enact or administer a federal program, and cannot “conscript state or local officers directly.”

Three county policies were at issue in the lawsuit, Behm laid out in her decision. First, the county prosecutor’s office directed prosecutors to consider immigration consequences when making charging decisions, as well as not to share information with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement beyond what would be required by federal law. Second, the county sheriff’s office instructed officers not to ask about immigration status and determined that the office would not detain individuals for ICE without a judicial warrant or court order. Finally, the county’s Board of Commissioners decided not to allow federal immigration officers onto county property if they did not have a judicial warrant or court order.

The federal government’s initial complaint alleged that the county “insists on obstructing federal immigration enforcement operations and shielding criminal offenders from apprehension by federal law enforcement. Washtenaw County’s policies aim to obstruct federal law enforcement and celebrate thwarting the constitutional obligation of the President of the United States to take care that federal immigration law be faithfully executed.”

The supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution has complicated local and state level responses to federal immigration enforcement for communities around the country that do not want ICE to have a presence.

One aspect of that legal doctrine is ‘obstacle preemption,” when state law serves as an obstacle to the purposes and objectives embodied in a federal law. The federal government argued Washtenaw County’s policies fit that definition. However, a high threshold must be met to prove that preemption.

Behm wrote that a refusal to cooperate with immigration enforcement “does not constitute discrimination against the federal government,” and therefore is not constitutionally prohibited.

Quoting from another court ruling, Behm added that a “healthy balance of power between the States and the Federal Government [reduces] the risk of tyranny and abuse from either front,” concluding that Washtenaw County had done nothing more than “exercise its constitutional authority under the Tenth Amendment.”

title: Deported to Equatorial Guinea with a large abdominal hernia: 'I'm not worth a dime'

text:
Faces have blurred with the days, as they slowly sank into the reality of waking up in America and suddenly finding themselves in Africa. On board an ICE Air flight that left Alexandria, Louisiana, on August 20, there was a man who, nevertheless, almost everyone will remember. “He’s Cuban, yes, a Cuban whose insides were bulging out of his belly,” says a young Colombian who cannot precisely identify what he saw. A Honduran on the same plane also noticed the protrusion showing through the other passenger’s stomach, “like it was intestine, everything was open, his belly sticking out.” When that man and four others refused to get off the plane in Liberia and were taken on to Equatorial Guinea, no one cared that he was ill and fell face-first onto the tarmac as he was shoved.

The man’s mother, Caridad, hasn’t been able to eat at home in Lehigh Acres, Florida. His sister, Dorty Sánchez, is desperate. One day they went on Facebook and watched a video from Equatorial Guinea. One of the people deported there reported that someone traveling with him was in very poor health. “He said there was a young man with an open belly and that his name was Leonardo Sánchez. And if he has an open belly and his name is Leonardo, then that’s my brother, it can’t be anyone else.”

That is how the family learned that Sánchez, who until now had been held in Texas, was even farther away from them despite being a lawful permanent U.S. resident. They say he had been arrested for drug possession and had been doing community service hours. Last year, at a gas station, he was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and initially taken to the Alligator Alcatraz facility. Since then, his mother and sister have done everything they could to get him out of detention. “We had hired a lawyer from the Wannamaker firm and, supposedly, there were options because of his medical condition.” But that lawyer, they say, scammed them, and now Sánchez is in a faraway place, his body aching, not knowing whether he will be able to have the surgery — his tenth — that is scheduled at Jackson Memorial Hospital.

“I’m not worth a dime,” Sánchez says, appearing on a video call with EL PAÍS from a room at the Bamy Hotel in the city of Malabo. The hotel is owned by the family of Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the country’s president, who has been in power for almost half a century. This month, several reports said some people were threatened at gunpoint in that hotel, where the government was also housing Ebola patients. For some time, the facility has also been hosting deportees who have arrived in the country as part of a $7.5 million agreement with the administration of Donald Trump.

Sánchez strokes his beard; he hasn’t been able to shave. They haven’t even given him a toothbrush, toothpaste, or clothes. Four days after his arrival, he was still wearing the same gray pants he left the United States in on the more than 36-hour flight alongside about 20 other deportees who were never told they were bound for Africa. During the trip they were given sandwiches and water they could barely bring to their mouths while remaining handcuffed and shackled. Sánchez says he wasn’t allowed to go to the bathroom the entire time. “I wet my pants three times,” he says.

As soon as he reached the hotel he washed his pants and the binder — the only one he has to support the bulge in his abdomen. Sánchez clutches his stomach constantly, as if holding himself together to stop his body from spilling apart. Nearly 10 years ago, in Hialeah, he was stabbed several times. “His intestine was damaged, he was in a coma for 40 days. The skin was left open and they had to graft it and put the colon to the side,” his sister says. Later, when he fell into ICE custody, he found his attackers had also been detained, but they were released. “They put the man who stabbed me in my same unit and then released him. I told the judge that,” he says.

That lump everyone notices on his stomach is a large abdominal hernia. Ever since he developed it, Sánchez has been unable to lift more than 20 pounds, has trouble finding work, and suffers from pain he finds unbearable. At the hotel — which is guarded by armed personnel and which they are not allowed to leave — he has only been given paracetamol to relieve the discomfort.

They also took him to a local hospital. “But at the hospital, they said that if I didn’t have any documents, the doctors wouldn’t take responsibility for me. They asked the officer who brought me there if he was responsible, and he said no, that he’d just been sent there. The doctor said, ‘If you won’t take responsibility, how are we supposed to?’” Sánchez recounts.

At a time when the U.S. government has signed deportation agreements with more than a dozen African countries, concern centers not only on the danger and legal limbo these people face but also on the medical care they receive. Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, a rights organization that has tracked these deportations, says they are “deeply concerned” about the situation in Equatorial Guinea. “People held in the hotel are deprived of access to essential medical care and subjected to conditions that further endanger their health and well-being, while suffering physical abuses by guards and being pressured to return precisely to the countries they fled to escape persecution or torture,” she says.

Over weeks of speaking with migrants of various nationalities sent to the Central African Republic, Liberia, and Equatorial Guinea, this newspaper confirmed that not only are they not receiving adequate medical care, but they can barely communicate with doctors in places where most people speak French. Some have reported stomach problems and allergies from the water or food. Others have experienced malarial episodes.

Pietro Lima, a 56-year-old Brazilian also deported to Equatorial Guinea, needs medication after losing 30% of his intestine and a kidney because of gunshot wounds sustained in his home country. “ICE had my medication on hand and I’ve been without it for five days; I need to take it. I spoke to people here and they know nothing about it,” he says.

When asked about Sánchez’s health and that of other migrants deported to Africa, a Department of Homeland Security spokesman told El PAÍS that “all of these undocumented migrants were deported to a safe third country.” “We are enforcing the law as written. If a judge determines an undocumented immigrant has no right to remain in this country, we will remove them. Period. The Trump administration is using every legal option to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, as President Trump promised,” the spokesman said. The State Department has not yet responded to this newspaper’s questions.

“This is human trafficking”

The flight that left Louisiana on August 20 made a refueling stop in Dakar, Senegal. It then continued to Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, a country that agreed to receive migrants under a $5 million deal with Washington. Pietro Lima, the Brazilian, never thought he would end up there. “Three days earlier, at the detention center, they tried to force me to sign a paper saying whether I wanted to go to Liberia and I didn’t sign it,” he says.

In Liberia, some migrants disembarked, but a small group refused to get off the plane. Pietro and the Cubans Darwin Hernández, Emilio Destrade, Carlos Rodríguez, and Leonardo Sánchez were prepared to do anything to avoid stepping into a territory they did not know. Through the plane windows they could see a large police deployment. “We told them we didn’t feel safe, but they forced us to get off. They carried me between four people and beat me while I was handcuffed,” Rodríguez says. Leonardo Sánchez was thrown down the aircraft stairs and landed on the tarmac with his hernia exposed.

The Cubans and the Brazilian began to protest. “We are not from Africa, we’re from another part of the world,” Rodríguez told them. Because of the commotion, they were returned to the plane, and ICE officers told them to remain calm, that they would take them back to the United States. The plane changed course and almost three hours later they were in Equatorial Guinea — an unprecedented incident, the first time a group of deportees has refused to disembark from an ICE plane and ended up somewhere else.

“How can a government, in the space of a few hours, send us to another country, and that country accept us?” Rodríguez asks. “This is human trafficking, they trafficked us on a plane.”

The government of Equatorial Guinea, which has been receiving deportees since late 2025, issued a statement saying it would treat “any national of a third country transferred by the Government of the United States of America to Equatorial Guinea consistently with its international legal obligations” and that they would not be “subjected to persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, nor to torture.”

Finally, the migrants arrived at Malabo International Airport, shortly after 8:00 p.m. According to Lima, they were taken down a rear part of the terminal, in the dark, away from the public eye. “To hide from people what was happening,” he says. “When the plane landed we asked ourselves: what place is this? Nobody told us anything. They asked us to get off and we still refused. But we saw more than 30 hooded police officers with weapons below. We were scared.”

Still handcuffed, they were taken by van to the Bamy Hotel, just a couple miles from the airport, about a 10-minute drive. “We are the only Latinos here,” Rodríguez says. “We are prisoners here. If we are free, as they say, why can’t we cook our food or go to the market to buy it?” To this day they have no identification, no passports or legal documents provided by Liberian or Equatorial Guinean authorities. They do not know what will happen to them.

Michael Flynn, executive director of the Global Detention Project, an organization that researches and documents the detention of migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees worldwide, told this newspaper that Equatorial Guinea “lacks an asylum framework to properly process refugee claims.” “Testimonies from detainees indicate they are not receiving safe or adequate food, that they are not being provided necessary medical treatment and that they have no clear idea what is happening to them or what their fate will be. The uncertainty must be truly agonizing,” he says. “The detention of these people is part of a deeply troubling trend in which migrants are deported from the United States to countries with which they have no significant ties, and then subjected to detention, often with little or no access to legal assistance or effective remedies.”

text:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to back its policy barring migrants who cross the U.S-Mexico border from applying for asylum.

In a petition, the administration says the policy the president issued on the first day of his second term in January 2025, which declared the situation at the southern border an invasion, has led to a drastic drop in illegal border crossings.

The petition asks the justices to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington that struck down the policy as unlawful in April, but allowed it to remain in effect as the Trump administration appealed.

That ruling, the Trump administration argues, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

Trending

Border Patrol saw an 84% drop in its encounters with migrants along the southern border in fiscal year 2025 compared to the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center. The figure is the lowest in more than 50 years.

“The proclamation and its asylum restrictions are thus critical pieces of American national and foreign policy; the judicial interference by the lower courts in the operation of those initiatives warrants this Court’s review,” the petition says.

A panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled the Immigration and Nationality Act doesn’t allow Trump to suspend people’s rights to apply for asylum or remove them from the country through processes outside of those outlined in the statute.

“Denying asylum in one stroke, without any information about the affected individuals, necessarily ignores every risk of persecution they face when forced back to where they came from,” the D.C. Circuit wrote. “The challenged decision thus necessarily denies asylum even to foreign individuals who are sure to face persecution without it.”

Faisal Al-Juburi, co-CEO of The Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, one of the groups suing the administration, said in a statement responding to the petition that the president isn’t above the law.

“By asking the Supreme Court to bypass laws that Congress passed to protect asylum seekers, the Trump administration is once again trying to seize unchecked power,” said Al-Juburi. “This isn’t just a policy disagreement. It’s a direct attack on our democracy and the checks and balances that keep us free.”

Las Americas Immigrant Advocacy Center, the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project and 13 migrants are the other plaintiffs in the lawsuit to stop the proclamation in February 2025.

text:
Aug. 25, 2026

By Isiah Holmes, Wisconsin Examiner

The Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) has joined 19 other states, including the commonwealths of Massachusetts and Virginia, in a lawsuit pushing back against the Trump administration’s attempts to attach immigration enforcement requirements to federal grants supporting state and local public safety efforts.

“Threatening to cut funding that supports law enforcement if states don’t agree to unlawful conditions is an abuse of the Trump administration’s authority,” Attorney General Josh Kaul said in a statement. “This funding should be distributed to the states, not improperly used as a bargaining chip.”

The lawsuit states that the grant programs, which have been active for decades, “provide more than a billion dollars to States annually to address some of the most serious threats to the safety of their residents: from gang violence to drug trafficking to sexual assault to all kinds of violent crimes.” The funds, which are enacted by Congress, are used “to assist more than 8.5 million crime victims; pay more than 200,000 claims for losses suffered by crime victims; and fund ongoing criminal justice and public safety operations, such as drug task forces, crisis intervention programs, and youth recidivism reduction efforts, in all 50 states and over 1,000 local government units nationwide,” the lawsuit states.

Under President Donald Trump, states which depend on these funds have been advised to either cooperate with Trump’s immigration priorities or face losing access to those funds. Calling this a “brazen attempt to manipulate critical funding for law enforcement and crime victims to strong-arm States into supporting the Administration’s civil immigration policies,” the lawsuit asserts that the Trump administration is running afoul with governing principles of the United States: that a federal agency “has no power to act … unless and until Congress confers power upon it.” Since Congress has the power of the purse, it decides what criteria executive branch agencies — like the Justice Department — must use when awarding grants, the suit argues.

The lawsuit also accuses the Trump administration of not considering how denying these grants would undermine public safety across the country. “Action by this Court is urgently needed,” the lawsuit states, asserting that it is illegal for the administration to impose these conditions on the public safety grants.

In a press release, the Wisconsin DOJ said Monday that last year the Trump administration declared that states wouldn’t be able to access Victims Crime Act funds unless they cooperated with the administration’s hardline deportation agenda, affecting $1.3 billion in grants.. A coalition of states sued and the administration reversed its action and released the money.

This year, however, the immigration conditions have been applied funding for juvenile justice and law enforcement, and amount to over $6 million in Wisconsin alone — a loss of $3.2 million in grant assistance, $2.1 million for a crisis intervention program, and $800,000 for juvenile justice and delinquency prevention, according to DOJ.

Although 20 sheriff offices across Wisconsin partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) through the 287(g) program, many communities have mixed relationships with the controversial federal agency. Some police departments may still cooperate with immigration enforcement even without an official 287(g) program. Others have policies prohibiting officers and jails from participating in immigration enforcement.

Despite public pushback, immigration agents have conducted surges and arrests in neighborhoods, courthouses, and elsewhere since Trump returned to office. In Milwaukee County, where some of these enforcement efforts have played out, local elected officials have enacted local ordinances and policies to curb the effect ICE operations have on public safety in the city. These, however, have invited further confrontation with the Trump administration.

The Trump administration has directed U.S. embassies and consulates around the world to postpone immigrant visa interviews while consular officers complete training on new public-charge guidance, temporarily stalling applications that have reached the interview stage.

The State Department told diplomatic posts to reschedule immigrant visa interviews until consular officers complete the training on how to evaluate whether an applicant is likely to become a public charge.

A public-charge determination can make an immigrant visa applicant inadmissible under federal immigration law if officials determine the person is likely to become dependent on certain forms of public assistance after arriving in the U.S.

"In early August, we launched a global training initiative at all of our embassies and consulates worldwide. To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted," a State Department official said in a statement.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES SIX-FIGURE PRICE TAG FOR NEW H-1B VISAS

The official added that the training is intended to ensure evaluations of visa applicants are made "comprehensively and consistently."

For most diplomatic posts, the training sessions are expected to take place this week.

The State Department did not say when affected applicants would be notified of their rescheduled interview dates.

The scheduling changes have sparked uncertainty among immigrant visa applicants who received emails informing them that their interviews had been canceled without instructions for immediately rescheduling them.

STATE DEPARTMENT BLASTS BACK AT 'ROGUE JUDGE' WHO OVERTURNED AGGRESSIVE VISA CRACKDOWN

Applicants were told they would receive future notice of a new interview date but were not given a timeline for when that communication could be expected.

The move comes as President Donald Trump pursues a broader immigration crackdown that has extended beyond illegal immigration to legal immigration pathways. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on curbing illegal immigration, his administration has also imposed additional restrictions on legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas and new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the U.S.

The administration has also pursued visa revocations and removal proceedings in cases involving political activity and speech, including some anti-Israel activists. Those efforts have prompted court challenges alleging violations of free-speech and due-process protections.

The administration said Monday that it was preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S., a move that would represent the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

On January 8, 2026, he was issued a Notice to Appear (NTA), the charging document in removal proceedings, and taken into immigration custody.
Twenty-six days later, on February 3, he appeared before the immigration court for his “initial master calendar hearing”, the first appearance in removal proceedings, which is similar to an arraignment in criminal court.
The court gave the respondent two more weeks to find a lawyer and reset the matter to March 2.
That said, Congress understood that there is a difference between a statutory right to counsel in removal proceedings and a real opportunity to find a lawyer.
Significantly, it found: The increase in the immigration court case backlog occurred as immigration courts completed fewer cases annually.
text:
On August 14, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) — the DOJ tribunal that reviews immigration decisions — issued an opinion in Matter of A-K-R-, concluding that an immigration judge (IJ) did not err in denying a third continuance to an alien respondent to find counsel, deeming the respondent’s request to file an asylum application abandoned, and ordering the respondent removed. Simply put, the Board concluded the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) requires IJs to give aliens 10 days to find a lawyer — no less, but no more either. If this precedent stands, it will advance what the Supreme Court has termed a “strong public interest” — and thereby remove a huge impediment to the smooth functioning of our immigration system.

A-K-R-

The respondent, identified only as “A-K-R-” to comply with regulations protecting the identity of aliens who have stated an intention to seek humanitarian protection, is an Indian national who entered the United States illegally at some point in the past.

On January 8, 2026, he was issued a Notice to Appear (NTA), the charging document in removal proceedings, and taken into immigration custody.

Twenty-six days later, on February 3, he appeared before the immigration court for his “initial master calendar hearing”, the first appearance in removal proceedings, which is similar to an arraignment in criminal court.

At that hearing, the IJ provided A-K-R- with the advisals required under 8 C.F.R. § 1240.10(a), and gave him two weeks to find an attorney or to file an application for “relief”, that is, an immigration benefit or protection that would allow him to remain in the United States.

Two weeks later, on February 17, A-K-R- appeared again before the IJ and requested more time to find counsel. The court gave the respondent two more weeks to find a lawyer and reset the matter to March 2.

On that date, respondent again appeared without an attorney. A-K-R- admitted the removal charges in the NTA and the IJ found he was removable as charged.

At that point, A-K-R- claimed a fear of harm if he were returned to India, and the IJ told him he may be eligible for asylum and the associated protections of statutory withholding of removal under section 241(b)(3) of the INA and withholding of removal under the Convention Against Torture (CAT).

Aliens submit the same form, I-589, “Application for Asylum and for Withholding of Removal” to apply for asylum, statutory withholding, and CAT, and the IJ reset the matter for 16 days, to March 18, for A-K-R- to either file that application or be ordered removed.

At that next hearing date, A-K-R- appeared without the I-589, complaining “he was unable to get any documents”, and requested yet another continuance.

The IJ denied that request and ordered the respondent removed from the United States.

A-K-R- filed an appeal with the BIA, contending the IJ erred in proceeding with his case because he had been “unable to contact an attorney or obtain documents to support his claim due to a lack of funds or people outside detention who could assist him” and that “he lacked the education necessary to complete an application for relief by himself”.

The “Right to Counsel” in Removal Proceedings

Section 292 of the INA governs an alien’s right to counsel in removal proceedings, and it provides that respondents “shall have the privilege of being represented (at no expense to the Government) by such counsel, authorized to practice in such proceedings, as [they] shall choose”.

In other words, aliens facing removal charges have a statutory right to counsel, but because removal proceedings are civil, not criminal, in nature, they do not have a right to free counsel provided by the government.

That said, a number of attorneys nationwide are willing to provide pro bono counsel at free or reduced rates for aliens in removal proceedings, and among the regulatorily mandated advisals IJs must provide respondents at initial master calendar hearings are the following:

[the] right to representation, at no expense to the government, by counsel of his or her own choice authorized to practice in the proceedings [and] the availability of pro bono legal services for the immigration court location at which the hearing will take place.

IJs are also required to “ascertain that the respondent has received a list of such pro bono legal service providers”, and in this case the immigration court complied with that regulatory requirement, as well.

“Securing of Counsel” under Section 239 of the INA

Those regulatory advisal mandates in 8 C.F.R. § 1240.10(a) are based on and mirror requirements in section 239 of the INA, the statutory provision that governs the issuance and service of NTAs.

Specifically, when DHS serves aliens with NTAs, section 239(a)(1)(E) of the INA requires officers to notify the respondents served that they “may be represented by counsel” and to provide them with “a current list of” pro bono counsel.

To make sure those pro bono provider lists are up-to-date, section 239(b)(2) of the INA requires DOJ to “provide for lists (updated not less often than quarterly) of persons who have indicated their availability to represent pro bono aliens” in removal proceedings under section 240 of the INA.

That said, Congress understood that there is a difference between a statutory right to counsel in removal proceedings and a real opportunity to find a lawyer.

Consequently, section 239(b)(1) of the INA (“Securing of counsel”), states that, “In order that an alien be permitted the opportunity to secure counsel before” the initial master calendar hearing, “the hearing date shall not be scheduled earlier than 10 days after the service of the notice to appear, unless the alien requests in writing an earlier hearing date”.

Keep that requirement in mind, because it is key to the BIA’s latest opinion.

“Continuances”

Technically, an IJ can issue a removal order at any point during removal proceedings, provided the court concludes that there are no additional issues for it to consider.

To ensure aliens can take advantage of their section 292 right to counsel and to otherwise protect the parties’ “due process” rights in removal proceedings, however, regulations at 8 C.F.R. § 1003.29 (“Continuances”) explicitly permit IJs to “grant a motion for continuance for good cause shown”.

The regulation never explains what “good cause” respondents must “show” to secure a continuance, however, which has been a major impediment to the expeditious completion of removal proceedings — and in turn a significant roadblock to the smooth functioning of our immigration system, because under section 241(a) of the INA, DHS usually needs an IJ removal order to deport any alien.

And IJs’ ability to quickly complete removal cases has been an issue for two decades, as the Government Accountability Office (GAO) concluded in a June 2017 report, “Immigration Courts. Actions Needed to Reduce Case Backlog and Address Long-Standing Management and Operational Challenges”.

GAO reported therein that between FY 2006 and FY 2015, immigration courts’ backlogs had increased 44 percent — even “while case receipts remained steady”.

Significantly, it found:

The increase in the immigration court case backlog occurred as immigration courts completed fewer cases annually. Specifically, the number of immigration court cases completed annually declined by 31 percent from fiscal year 2006 to fiscal year 2015 — from about 287,000 cases completed in fiscal year 2006 to about 199,000 completed in 2015.

GAO determined the “median initial case completion time”, i.e., the period between the filing of the NTA and the point at which IJs issued final decisions, had increased more than 500 percent over that period, “from 43 days in fiscal year 2006 to 286 days in fiscal year 2015”.

One key reason why case completions were taking so much longer, the GAO concluded, was because IJs were granting more continuances.

GAO explained that “the use of all types of continuances increased by 23 percent” during that period, and that “9 percent of cases completed in fiscal year 2006 experienced four or more continuances compared to 20 percent of cases completed in fiscal year 2015”.

Axiomatically, GAO noted that “cases with multiples continuances took longer to complete than cases with no or fewer continuances”.

Having done the job, I can assure you most IJs weren’t granting multiple continuances because they were lazy; they granted them because the continuance regulation was vague and denying a continuance exposed an IJ to a finding by the BIA and/or circuit court on review that the judge had denied the alien due process — a black mark on any jurist’s record.

Matter of C-B-

Precedent wasn’t much help, either, which brings me to Matter of C-B-, a 2012 opinion in which the BIA held IJs “must grant” respondents “a reasonable and realistic period of time to provide a fair opportunity for the respondent to seek, speak with, and retain counsel” prior to proceeding, particularly where the alien has indicated an intent to seek asylum, statutory withholding, or CAT.

On the one hand, that’s common sense, and it should be noted that the respondent there (C-B-) was ordered removed at his initial master calendar hearing, where he was detained and unrepresented.

At that hearing, C-B- initially told the IJ he didn’t want a lawyer but instead wanted to be ordered removed but then changed his mind and stated he wanted time to find counsel “because he had a son”.

As the Board explained, the IJ “did not ask for clarification regarding the respondent’s request for a continuance to seek counsel; nor did she rule on the request for a continuance. Instead, she proceeded to take pleadings and find the respondent removable.”

On the other hand, however, “a reasonable and realistic period of time to provide a fair opportunity for the respondent to seek, speak with, and retain counsel” is as vague a standard as “good cause shown”.

Matter of A-K-R-

While the Board in Matter of C-B- cited sections 292 and 240(b)(4)(A) of the INA — the latter of which essentially repeats section 292’s language on the right to counsel at no expense to the government — it never referenced the “securing of counsel” language in section 239(b)(1) of the act at all.

Which brings me to Matter of A-K-R-, where the BIA corrected that oversight and gave IJs the “brightline rule” they’ve needed for decades in deciding whether to grant aliens’ motions to continue their removal hearings for counsel.

Reading the act in toto, the Board concluded that “the only statutory or regulatory time requirement ... necessary to safeguard an alien’s privilege of legal counsel is that the first hearing may not be scheduled earlier than 10 days after service of the notice to appear as set forth in section 239(b)(1) of the” INA.

Consequently, the BIA concluded that the portions of its opinion in Matter of C-B- “regarding the legal standard it purported to create with respect to the right to counsel departed from the text of the statute and is dicta”, and for that reason the Board “withdrew” from any implication that they “set[] forth a statutory or regulatory mandate”.

Simply put, the BIA in Matter of A-K-R- held that Congress in section 239(b)(1) of the INA gave aliens in removal proceedings 10 days to find a lawyer, and while IJs in specific situations may give them more time for counsel, nothing in the act or regulations requires them to do so.

To close the loop, the Board also dismissed A-K-R-‘s claim that he should have been given additional time to find an attorney to help him complete the I-589, noting that he failed to “include any specifics as to what diligent steps he took, if any, to complete the application or find assistance to do so”.

The Application for Asylum and Withholding of Removal is deliberately simple, written in such a way to allow pro se applicants to complete it, and as I have explained in the past, the asylum statute provides that an applicant’s testimony alone “may be sufficient to sustain the applicant's burden without corroboration, but only if the applicant satisfies the trier of fact that the applicant's testimony is credible, is persuasive, and refers to specific facts sufficient to demonstrate that the applicant is a refugee”.

Will It Stand?

As the Supreme Court has held, there’s a “strong public interest in bringing” immigration cases “to a close as promptly as is consistent with the interest in giving the adversaries a fair opportunity to develop and present their respective cases”. The BIA’s opinion in Matter of A-K-R- advances that “strong public interest”.

That is, it will do so, if Article III circuit courts don’t strike it down first.

As the BIA explained: “The Fifth Circuit, in whose jurisdiction this case arises, has assumed without deciding that, while aliens do not have a Sixth Amendment right to counsel, they may have a Fifth Amendment due process right to counsel.”

Because the IJ denied A-K-R- a third continuance more than six weeks after his initial master calendar hearing, and more than two months after he was first served with his NTA, the Fifth Circuit will likely conclude he had sufficient time to find counsel, and dismiss any due process claim he might bring.

That said, a similar case, in which an IJ denies an alien’s motion for continuance for counsel on a shorter timeframe, may present a more complicated due process challenge for the government. Some degree of IJ prudence and discretion will still be in order, Matter of A-K-R- notwithstanding.

Why Only Now?

Congress first limited aliens to 10 days to find counsel when it amended section 239(b)(1) of the INA in 1996, which raises the question why it took the BIA nearly three decades to apply that restriction.

The likely answer is as disheartening as it is simple: There are hundreds of thousands of words in the INA, and most DHS attorneys and DOJ adjudicators are only really familiar with the ones they use daily, such as the asylum standards in section 208 of the act and the removal proceeding rules in section 240.

To be fair, there were a lot of INA amendments in that 1996 act, and the then-INS and the immigration courts didn’t have a lot of time to digest them all. And as the recent legal folderol over the Trump administration’s “mass detention” policy (also based on 1996 changes) reveals, courts are “reluctant” (to put it charitably) at this late date to permit the implementation of the strictest ones.

Bottlenecks

For decades, respondents in immigration court have used serial continuances to stretch their removal cases out indefinitely, thus stymieing DHS’s ability to deport them. On August 14, DOJ’s appellate review board put an end to that practice — for now — and put aliens in proceedings on notice that, if they want legal representation, the clock is ticking.

title: ICE Wants the Country's Voter Data - 404 Media
authors: Joseph Cox, Matthew Gault, Jason Koebler
description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is looking for a federal contractor to provide it with access to the country’s voter registration and voter history data, according to newly released procurement records reviewed by 404 Media.
The procurement records say ICE is seeking the data to help detect fraud.
Specifically, ICE is seeking “Public voter registration file for each Government-identified jurisdiction,” and “Public voter history file for each Government-specified federal election, when publicly available and separate from the public voter registration file.” Voter data is public by design and can be obtained in various ways.
But constant claims that voter fraud is happening on a wider scale or tangibly impacting elections runs the risk of disenfranchising voters from participating at all.
In July, 404 Media reported ICE was to pay Thomson Reuters $125 million for access to a wealth of personal data to investigate “voter fraud.” Personal data Thomson Reuters holds includes peoples’ names, addresses, Social Security numbers, ethnicity, and more.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is looking for a federal contractor to provide it with access to the country’s voter registration and voter history data, according to newly released procurement records reviewed by 404 Media.

The procurement records say ICE is seeking the data to help detect fraud. But given the administration’s habit of using fraud as a pretense for large immigration enforcement actions, and President Trump’s constant comments about election security in the lead up to the midterms, the planned hiring of a contractor to handle voter data raises questions around what exactly ICE plans to do with the data.

“The purpose of this acquisition is for the handling and secure delivery of publicly available voter registration files and voter history files to support Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) fraud detection and data segmentation activities,” a section of the procurement records reads. The records are part of a Request for Information, or RFI, which means the government is asking potentially capable contractors to come forward.

The records say the list of jurisdictions ICE wants voter data from is likely to be limited at first, but that the contractor needs to have the capability to get data from all 50 states and other U.S. territories.

Specifically, ICE is seeking “Public voter registration file for each Government-identified jurisdiction,” and “Public voter history file for each Government-specified federal election, when publicly available and separate from the public voter registration file.”

Voter data is public by design and can be obtained in various ways. Some sites collate this data and make it easily searchable.

But handling such a large volume of data in a clean and reliable manner could be a challenge. ICE is looking for a contractor to essentially help streamline that process, by both obtaining the data and handling it for the agency.

The purchase specifically is for HSI, the part of ICE traditionally focused on criminal investigations, including money laundering, cybercrime, and various types of fraud. That does include voter fraud.

Earlier this month, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) highlighted an HSI case that ended in charges against a Chinese national for alleged fraudulent voter registration and fraudulent voting.

Experts generally agree that voter fraud is exceptionally rare. But constant claims that voter fraud is happening on a wider scale or tangibly impacting elections runs the risk of disenfranchising voters from participating at all.

In July, 404 Media reported ICE was to pay Thomson Reuters $125 million for access to a wealth of personal data to investigate “voter fraud.” Personal data Thomson Reuters holds includes peoples’ names, addresses, Social Security numbers, ethnicity, and more.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

text:
More than 45,000 people were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last month, the highest number since Donald Trump retook office, according to data the Deportation Data Project released Monday.

In total, since Trump’s inauguration last year, ICE has detained over 610,000 people — more than the population of Atlanta, Baltimore, Milwaukee or the entire state of Wyoming.

At times, previous administrations, both Democratic and Republican, have booked hundreds of thousands of people into ICE custody for processing. But in Trump’s second term, the number of people ICE booked and then held for extended periods of time has ballooned.

Last year, more than 270,000 people spent at least a week detained, surpassing any other year since 2012, the earliest in the Deportation Data Project’s archive. However, even as Trump's enforcement upends lives and livelihoods in immigrant communities, the number of people detained and deported falls far short of the president's goal of deporting 1 million people per year.

The Trump administration’s policy is to detain almost all unauthorized immigrants, regardless of their individual circumstances, and to keep them detained as long as it takes for their cases to move through immigration court — often months, or even years.

Both the Biden and Obama administrations oversaw enormous spikes in book-ins to ICE detention amid increases in migrants arriving at the Southern border, including unaccompanied children in 2012 and single adults in 2023. Many of those people were not locked up for long; instead, they were processed and then released to the community — where it is easier to challenge their deportations — while their cases played out in immigration courts.

Since Trump returned to office, border crossings have dropped precipitously. And yet ICE detentions, especially long-term, remain among the highest in the timeframe covered by the data.

The other major difference between today’s immigration detention machine and that of prior administrations, including Trump’s first term, is where and how the arrests and detentions are taking place.

About 80% of people detained since Trump retook office have come from the interior of the country, where they are much more likely to have community ties — families, jobs, homes — than those crossing the border. That’s almost a complete reversal of the practice during the previous two years under President Joe Biden, when 30% of detentions came from inside the U.S.

“What we’re seeing is something unprecedented,” said Caitlin Patler, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley who studies immigration. “Going after people where they work, where they pray, in the streets, at the schools. These are these places that in the past you wouldn't really have seen ICE arrests happening at scale.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, a professor who studies immigration at Ohio State University Moritz College of Law, warned of the lasting impact on a generation of people in the cities hit hardest by Trump’s immigration tactics, like Chicago and Minneapolis.

“People who are detained lose their jobs, lose their homes, lose the money that is needed to pay for food, medical care, school supplies,” Hernández says. “Those are the kind of direct impacts that don’t go away the moment the refrigerator is stocked again, or the electricity is paid.”

Others, who are deported, are not able to return to their homes at all.

“The administration lost a lot of goodwill from a lot of people who thought they were going to remove bad people,” said Sarah Saldaña, who served as director of ICE from 2014 to 2017. “They've done everything to make it look like a lawless-enforcement agency.”

Some people arrested and detained in the last year had already been released from custody by judges during previous administrations with agreements to attend their immigration court hearings.

For many of these people, nothing about their lives or cases has changed to warrant incarceration, said Amy Romero, an immigration attorney with the Lawyers' Committee for Rhode Island, who is representing many people in this situation.

“The only thing that’s changed is we now have an administration that is hell-bent on imprisoning as many immigrants as possible,” she said.

text:
Reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in several Connecticut communities, including Danbury, Stamford and Bridgeport, are raising concerns among residents and local officials.

Eyewitnesses in Danbury reported seeing federal agents in the city and witnessing arrests in recent days.

Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves said he is angry and concerned about the reported arrests and detentions and the impact they may be having on families.

"There are children who are afraid they're going to get home and their parents aren't there," Alves said. "There are kids who were at home yesterday and a parent never returned."

Connecticut Students for a Dream said it has been working with rapid response groups across the state to gather information about detentions. The organization said its network received firsthand reports from eyewitnesses indicating that at least 21 people were detained, including 16 in Danbury, four in Stamford and one in Bridgeport.

NBC Connecticut has reached out to ICE to confirm those figures but has not yet received a response.

Alves is urging residents to understand their legal rights, including when they are required to open their doors to law enforcement.

"People should know that they don't have to open their door unless that law enforcement agency has a warrant and has a reason to talk to them," Alves said.

Seth Garben of Greater Danbury Area Unites for Immigrants said enforcement activity appeared to increase this week.

"Things really started heating up again yesterday," Garben said.

Video provided to NBC Connecticut by Al Robinson of HatCity Blog appears to show agents wearing vests labeled "Immigration and Customs Enforcement."

Alves said city officials are typically not notified before agents arrive in Danbury.

"They don't let us know if they're going to be here. We don't work with them. They don't work with us," Alves said.

ICE said in response to NBC Connecticut:

For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations.

title: Federal Judge Vacates 75-Country Immigrant Visa Ban: What Applicants and Employers ...
description:
A federal judge has struck down the State Department policy that halted immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries.
The suspension affected both family-sponsored and employment-based immigrant visa applicants processing through U.S. embassies and consulates abroad.
First, consular officers—not the Secretary of State—are charged with deciding whether an individual immigrant visa applicant is eligible under the law.
The court vacated the policy and set aside immigrant visa refusals that were based solely on the 75-country suspension.
That is meaningful relief for many families and workers whose immigrant visa cases were stopped by the 75-country policy.
text:
A federal judge has struck down the State Department policy that halted immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries. The August 21, 2026 decision in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio removes a major barrier for families and employment-based applicants who had otherwise qualified for immigrant visas but were refused solely because of their nationality.

The ruling is significant, but it does not mean that every affected case will be approved immediately. It restores individualized visa adjudication. Applicants must still satisfy all statutory and regulatory requirements, and separate restrictions may continue to apply.

What Was the 75-Country Policy?

Effective January 21, 2026, the Department of State suspended immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 designated countries while it reviewed screening and vetting policies related to the “public charge” ground of inadmissibility. The affected countries included Brazil, Colombia, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Russia, Jamaica, Nigeria, and many countries across Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe.

Under the policy, a consular officer could determine that an applicant was otherwise eligible for an immigrant visa and still refuse issuance based solely on the applicant’s nationality. The suspension affected both family-sponsored and employment-based immigrant visa applicants processing through U.S. embassies and consulates abroad.

Several nonprofit organizations, affected applicants, and U.S. citizen sponsors challenged the policy in federal court.

What Did the Court Decide?

U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas of the Southern District of New York concluded that the nationality-based suspension exceeded the Secretary of State’s authority and violated the Immigration and Nationality Act.

The court emphasized two features of the statutory framework. First, consular officers—not the Secretary of State—are charged with deciding whether an individual immigrant visa applicant is eligible under the law. Second, Section 202(a)(1)(A) of the Immigration and Nationality Act generally prohibits discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas because of a person’s nationality, place of birth, or place of residence.

The court vacated the policy and set aside immigrant visa refusals that were based solely on the 75-country suspension. As a result, the State Department must return to case-by-case adjudication rather than deny an otherwise eligible applicant merely because the applicant is a national of one of the designated countries.

What the Ruling Means in Practice

For an applicant whose immigrant visa was refused only under the 75-country policy, the decision may create a path for the case to be reconsidered. Applicants should not assume, however, that a consulate will reopen or approve a case automatically. The Department of State must first implement the ruling, and the government may seek appellate review or a stay.

The decision also does not eliminate the public charge ground of inadmissibility. Consular officers may continue to evaluate whether an applicant is likely to become a public charge based on the governing law and the applicant’s individual circumstances. Affidavits of support, household income, assets, job offers, health coverage, and other financial evidence may therefore remain important, depending on the immigrant visa category and the facts of the case.

For employment-based cases, employers and sponsored workers should confirm whether a refusal was based solely on the now-vacated policy or whether the consular officer identified an additional ground of inadmissibility or administrative processing. A refusal supported by another independent legal ground was not necessarily set aside by the court’s order.

Recommended Next Steps

Applicants, sponsoring family members, and employers with affected cases should consider the following:

Review the refusal record. Locate the refusal letter, CEAC status, consular correspondence, and any reference to the 75-country policy or the public charge ground of inadmissibility.

Confirm whether another restriction applies. Nationality-based restrictions under Presidential Proclamation 10998, administrative processing, documentary deficiencies, or a separate inadmissibility finding may still prevent issuance.

Keep financial evidence current. Updated employment letters, tax records, affidavits of support, proof of assets, and other evidence may be requested when adjudication resumes.

Watch for post-specific instructions. Consulates may differ in how and when they reopen or reconsider affected cases. Avoid submitting duplicate applications or paying new fees unless instructed.

Get case-specific advice before acting. The right strategy may depend on the refusal code, visa category, priority date, country of chargeability, and whether the government appeals or obtains a stay.

The Bottom Line

The court’s decision removes the State Department’s blanket nationality-based bar and restores the individualized adjudication required by federal immigration law. That is meaningful relief for many families and workers whose immigrant visa cases were stopped by the 75-country policy.

Even so, the ruling is not an automatic visa approval, and its practical effect will depend on implementation by the Department of State and any further court proceedings. Applicants and employers should review affected cases promptly, preserve all consular records, and obtain individualized guidance before taking the next step.

Because implementation will unfold over the coming weeks and each case presents its own facts, individuals and employers with cases affected by the 75-country policy should seek guidance from qualified immigration counsel to understand how the ruling applies to their specific circumstances.

Shapiro hires ex-Trump admin official to help counter president’s ‘attacks’ Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., is being paid $89 an hour.

text:
Shapiro hires ex-Trump admin official to help counter president’s ‘attacks’

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., is being paid $89 an hour.

This story was originally published by Spotlight PA.

HARRISBURG — Earlier this spring, with no public notice, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro made an unconventional hire: a senior advisor to help him deal with the Trump administration.

Jennifer Higgins, a longtime federal immigration official based in Washington, D.C., was brought on to help Shapiro and state agencies under his jurisdiction map out responses to some of the president’s targeted attacks on Democrat-led states — notably, funding cuts and demands for sensitive or proprietary information.

Higgins is being paid by the hour — an unusual arrangement for a gubernatorial staffer, and one that Shapiro’s office could not immediately explain. State payroll records show she is paid $89 per hour, and Shapiro officials said she works full-time, putting her annual salary at roughly $185,000.

The administration defended hiring Higgins, even though Pennsylvania already spends tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars every year for a federal government liaison.

The governor’s office employs a full-time lobbyist in Washington, D.C., who is paid $177,507 annually. And in theory, Pennsylvania’s two senators act as the state’s de facto protectors in the nation’s capital and run interference with the White House when problems arise.

But Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky explained in an emailed statement that an additional person was needed because “the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on the rights and freedoms of Pennsylvanians are reaching into every corner of our Commonwealth.”

Higgins, Lapowsky said, brings “deep expertise and invaluable perspective helping protect Pennsylvanians during this critical moment.” (Higgins did not respond to Spotlight PA’s request to speak with her directly.)

Still, Higgins’ expertise is in the immigration sphere, where she has spent nearly the entirety of her career. The governor’s office acknowledged that Higgins is not directly advising Shapiro on immigration issues, but is part of a larger group of policy officials, lawyers, and others who provide the governor with information on that and other issues facing the state.

Asked for an example of Higgins’ work, Lapowsky said she helped coordinate Shapiro’s response to a Trump administration demand that states turn over commercial driver’s license records containing personal information. Trump officials have pointed, among other things, to crashes involving noncitizen drivers as one reason for the crackdown and have threatened to withhold federal funding if states do not comply.

In August, Shapiro joined a coalition of state attorneys general suing the federal government over the subpoena.

It’s true that, since reclaiming the White House in 2024, President Donald Trump has used the levers of the federal government to punish blue states.

The administration admitted in a federal court filing this summer that it recommended scrapping billions in grants for clean-energy projects based solely on those states’ “political identity,” and whether Trump won the vote in those places in the 2024 election.

Earlier this year, Trump attempted to freeze billions in childcare and social assistance for five Democratic-led states — he had initiated the move following the federal fraud probe involving Minnesota’s social services network — which he later abandoned.

And Politico reported last month that Trump overruled his own emergency management agency to deny federal relief funds to four Democratic-led states.

For his part, Shapiro often talks about how his administration has sued Trump dozens of times to challenge the loss of federal funding. Those suits involve a range of initiatives, from education to natural disasters. The governor’s office also noted that unlike in other states, where attorneys general are handling litigation against Trump, Shapiro’s lawyers are taking on that work in Pennsylvania. Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, has not entered the commonwealth into any lawsuit against the president or his administration.

Many of those suits predate Higgins’ arrival, and were handled by attorneys already on Shapiro’s staff. But the volume of attacks coming from Washington, Lapowsky said, combined with the range and breadth of policies and issues being targeted, necessitated another person to help coordinate plans to respond.

Immigration leadership

Higgins’ role in the Shapiro administration differs significantly from the work that has defined her career.

She started as an immigration officer in the early 2000s, but quickly moved into leadership roles within the federal office that handles asylum applications and screenings and adjudicates refugee applications, according to an online biography.

Shortly after Trump was elected to a first term in 2016, Higgins became the office’s associate director. Some rights groups have highlighted that part of her bio, since she held a leadership position during the implementation of one of the federal government’s most controversial immigration programs.

Officially called the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP), but better known as Remain in Mexico, the program went into effect in early 2019. It required asylum seekers along the southern border to return to cities in Mexico, many of which are dangerous, while waiting for their immigration cases to be heard in the courts. Previously, those people were allowed to stay in the United States during that waiting period.

The Trump administration sold MPP as a way to thwart people with fraudulent claims from easily entering the U.S. But human rights and immigration groups, as well as multiple news organizations, extensively documented how migrants sent to Mexican border towns faced extreme danger, including kidnapping, assault, and rape. Tent camps were set up to house some of the asylum seekers, but living conditions were squalid, with no running water or electricity.

Human rights groups also noted that access to legal representation was fraught with obstacles, and resulted in higher numbers of cases being denied, sometimes just because migrants did not receive timely notices of their hearings or could not safely reach ports of entry into the country to be present for such hearings.

The office where Higgins held a senior leadership role at the time — the Refugee, Asylum and International Operations Directorate (RAIO) inside the U.S. Department of Homeland Security — was part of the larger apparatus tasked with the MPP’s rollout. Higgins’ level of involvement in the program’s operations is not clear, as the office’s work is subject to high levels of confidentiality. But the office she helped oversee is responsible for, among other duties, conducting asylum screenings and applications, according to its website. Its employees would have been at the front lines of the program’s implementation.

President Joe Biden ended the Remain in Mexico program after defeating Trump in 2020. Since retaking the White House, Trump officials have attempted to revive it but have been blocked by the courts.

During Biden’s presidency, Higgins continued to rise. She became acting chief of staff to then-U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, and within a year was appointed acting director of the department’s vast agency that oversees the legal U.S. immigration system.

Shortly after Trump started his second term, she was replaced.

text:
With immigration arrests spiking last month to all-time highs, a new state law took effect in New York stopping local cops from signing cooperation agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

The ban also sets up a confrontation between Gov. Kathy Hochul and her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman.

Blakeman is one of two county executives in New York who has so far refused to nullify a cooperation agreement with ICE.

"No county executive should think that they are above the law in the state of New York," Hochul said.

It was a stern warning to Blakeman as the new law went into effect preventing local cops from working with federal immigration agents to advance the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda.

Nassau County is one of only two of the state's 62 counties that have so far refused to comply with the law.

Within minutes of Hochul's remarks, New York Attorney General Letitia James issued subpoenas to law enforcement agencies that either did not confirm plans to unwind their agreements, or whose responses were deemed unsatisfactory.

The subpoenas went out to the sheriff's offices of Broome, Steuben, Nassau and Rensselaer counties, as well as the Nassau County Police Department.

A spokesman for Blakeman said the county executive would have no comment on the subpoenas, but at a recent appearance with President Trump, Blakeman vigorously defended working with ICE to rid the county of what he said were some 2,000 illegal immigrants with criminal records.

"Kathy Hochul, where do you want those guns? What neighborhood do you want to destroy? Where do you want those drugs? What community do you want to destroy? Where do you want those illegal immigrants with criminal records to live? You want it back in New York? We say no," Blakeman said at the time.

Defenders of the law stood in front of the Nassau Police Department to back up Hochul, who wants local police to reduce crime in their neighborhoods.

"Say it loud, say it clear, immigrants are welcome here," they chanted.

Hochul has said law enforcement will assist ICE "only if a real crime has been committed," not on civil immigration matters.

"Because we need local cops hunting down criminals, not kindergartners. Breaking up drug rings, not breaking up families. Arresting gun runners, not grandmas," Hochul said.

The subpoenas issued by James are the first step in forcing Nassau and the others to sever ties with ICE. A spokesperson said that if they don't comply, the next step would be a civil suit.

Last month, ICE agents arrested nearly 50,000 people. That's a 70% increase from February, in the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota that sparked protests.
